questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/3fe3ec24f8f8006f22bde8ba2dc39fd3cd3f73668b06f8ea4a74e4ed5206a193.png)

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/2a20f2651c24e48871028b44fe61da4600d632481877ef32ccdfd3241262a53b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1ba7c02f254313a73a813e4e43c44c25523ce77dd47e594a1db3b412a6bd5c3d.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 4,\,\,0\le x\le 5-y-\frac{z}{2}\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{5-y-z/2}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=5-y-z/2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{10-2y-z}(5-y-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{1}{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{z}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy & =[2y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =6-0 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

${∭}_{R}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dV$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/0008ba406cfe8a5b61d683a6854260897cb441752a5333add281ab1279e31b0b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2-\frac{y}{3}+z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/bbe6b6b897e5d53421080ae8e8b9dc49f2ea1b7e135f8426ee3f11af01cc2401.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le 2-\frac{y}{3}+z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2-y/3+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}(2-\frac{y}{3}+z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}{[z]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy & =[y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/ca994203c4a3889949e3452f48ea3f7295a152c5d9d4c809758f152d7115cedf.png)

Given that $R$ is the type II region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V=$
questions.worked_solution:
For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/a39d7a27f20283b6e6814db926801f16e3e2cb42c7fe16487350b536d3b63d3c.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-(y-1)^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/5058493860a1c4d919e3cd6786bb1aca156ae83d47f766c087e351e9764929c4.png)

Hence, $D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le 1-(y-1)^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡z[{x}^{2}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}3\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/2427e053c0e2d808b32db5d7fedf81365e7e50f0b3f2dc61598ad1795394686e.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2+2y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(2+2y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{y}^{2}z+2{y}^{3}z-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the missing limits in the repeated integral below

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}V
= 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
f(x,y,z) \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y
$$

where $R$ is the type II region defined as

$$
R=\left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 4, \: -y^2 \leq z \leq \sqrt{y}, \: -2 \leq x \leq ye^{z+2} \right\}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z)  \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: u_1(y,z) \leq x \leq u_2(y,z) \big\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm d V = \iint\limits_{D} \left[\int_{u_1(y,z)}^{u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm{d}x \right]\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
u_1(y,z) = -2, \qquad u_2(y,z)  = ye^{z+2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{-2}^{ye^{z+2}} f(x,y,z) \: \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D =\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 4, \: -y^2 \leq z \leq \sqrt{y} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating a Mixed Integral
canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{0}^{z} \dfrac{\cos (2y)}{1-y} \,\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (y,z) \, : \, 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \: 0 \leq z \leq 2\sqrt{1-y} \right\}.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}[x]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{\int }_{0}^{2\sqrt{1-y}}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2\sqrt{1-y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(\frac{4(1-y)}{2}-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region
canonical_examples.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 4x^3  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: 0 \leq x \leq \sqrt{y} \right\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the line $z = 4-y$ in the first quadrant.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} 4x^3 \, \textrm{d}V
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}} 4x^3 \, \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}4{x}^{3}\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{4}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{y}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{(\sqrt{y})}^{4}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/3c8712fa0a30ad94f503efe5e080ee89f83eb21f19fba45033bbedeab08ac816.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{y}^{2}z]_{z=0}^{z=4-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{2}(4-y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}4{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}(64-0)-\frac{1}{4}(256-0) \\  & =\frac{64}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 12z^2 \: \mathrm{d}V$

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/f25c393f10c35ffd9b4fa91cdf672a516cf6cff974a8aa563d350619a64b79bd.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
\iiint \limits_{R}  12z^2  \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{3-y-z}  12z^2  \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=3-y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}(3-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12{z}^{3}-4y{z}^{3}-3{z}^{4}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12-4y-3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy & =[9y-2{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(9-2)-0 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Skipping the Intermediate Step
tutorials.problem:
When writing down a triple integral as a repeated integral, we can often skip the intermediate step of expressing our triple integral as a mixed integral.

For example, suppose we wish to evaluate

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z)  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type II region given by 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: {\color{red}a} \leq y \leq {\color{red}b}, \: {\color{blue}v_1(y)} \leq z \leq {\color{blue}v_2(y)}, \: {\color{purple}u_1(y,z)} \leq x \leq {\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} \right\}.
$$

Notice that the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane is a type I plane region. Therefore, we can immediately express our triple integral as a repeated integral as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{\color{red}a}^{\color{red}b} \int_{\color{blue}v_1(y)}^{\color{blue}v_2(y)} \int_{\color{purple}u_1(y,z)}^{\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

observed_steps.name: Example: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z)  \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: u_1(y,z) \leq x \leq u_2(y,z) \big\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm d V = \iint\limits_{D} \left[\int_{u_1(y,z)}^{u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm{d}x \right]\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
u_1(y,z) = -2, \qquad u_2(y,z)  = ye^{z+2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{-2}^{ye^{z+2}} f(x,y,z) \: \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D =\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 4, \: -y^2 \leq z \leq \sqrt{y} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=(3y-z)^{2}\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={e}^{y+4z}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{(3y-z)^{2}}^{{e}^{y+4z}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,(3y−z)2≤x≤ey+4z}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dx]dA
b
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∫(3y−z)2ey+4z[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
d
∫(3y−z)2ey+4z[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dz
e
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=(3y−z)2u2(y,z)=ey+4z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dx]dA.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-3\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=5{y}^{4}+2.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-3}^{5{y}^{4}+2}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,−3≤x≤5y4+2}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dz
b
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
c
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
d
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA
e
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=−3u2(y,z)=5y4+2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/a905e1f60fb0aa865c071fcbccbfecb30dcac7a74b4b647d24a40f4c89ff1935.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-2y-1,\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={y}^{2}+2z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-8\le y\le {sin}^{2}⁡z,\,0\le z\le \pi \}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=0+\pi =\pi .
$$

The triple integral ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∫ab∫∗∗∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dxdydz is defined over the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):−8≤y≤sin2⁡z,0≤z≤π,−2y−1≤x≤y2+2z}. What is a+b?

a
sin2⁡z+π−8
b
y2+2z−2y−1
c
sin2⁡z−8
d
π
e
y2+2z−2y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have

u1(y,z)=−2y−1,u2(y,z)=y2+2z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dA.

Now, the region D is given by D={(x,y):−8≤y≤sin2⁡z,0≤z≤π}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get ∬D[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dA=∫0π∫−8sin2⁡z[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dydz=∫0π∫−8sin2⁡z∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dxdydz.

Finally, a+b=0+π=π.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/a905e1f60fb0aa865c071fcbccbfecb30dcac7a74b4b647d24a40f4c89ff1935.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-\sqrt{y+z},\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=4.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-z\le y\le 1,\,4\le z\le 5\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{4}^{5}{\int }_{-z}^{1}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{5}{\int }_{-z}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=4+5=9.
$$

{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-y-z}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le y\le z,\,2\le z\le 3\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-y-z}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{z}[{\int }_{-y-z}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{z}{\int }_{-y-z}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{4}}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=-2+z=z-2.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The triple integral ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∫∗∗∫ab∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dxdydz is defined over the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):−2≤y≤z,2≤z≤3,−y−z≤x≤y2+z4}. What is a+b?

a
y2+z4+y+z
b
5
c
y2+z4−y−z
d
z−2
e
z+3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have

u1(y,z)=−y−z,u2(y,z)=y2+z4.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

Now, the region D is given by D={(x,y):−2≤y≤z,2≤z≤3}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get ∬D[∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dA=∫23∫−2z[∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dydz=∫23∫−2z∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dxdydz.

Finally, a+b=−2+z=z−2.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}[x]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{\int }_{0}^{2\sqrt{1-y}}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2\sqrt{1-y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(\frac{4(1-y)}{2}-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Evaluating a Mixed Integral
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{0}^{z} \dfrac{\cos (2y)}{1-y} \,\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (y,z) \, : \, 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \: 0 \leq z \leq 2\sqrt{1-y} \right\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}[x]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{\int }_{0}^{2\sqrt{1-y}}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2\sqrt{1-y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(\frac{4(1-y)}{2}-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y{z}^{2}}\frac{12}{z}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{12}{z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{12}{z}(y{z}^{2}-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12yz\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}12yz\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2y}}12yz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[6y{z}^{2}]_{z=1}^{z=\sqrt{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6y((\sqrt{2y})^{2}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6y(2y-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}12{y}^{2}-6y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[4{y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =4(8-1)-3(4-1) \\  & =19\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}4xz\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}[2z{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2z({z}^{2}-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2y}}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{4-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{4-2y)})^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(4-2y)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(16-16y+4{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}8-8y+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[8y-4{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =16-16+\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the mixed integral ∬D[∫0z4xzdx]dA where the region D in the yz-plane is given by D={(y,z):0≤y≤2,0≤z≤4−2y}.

EXPLANATION

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∬D[∫0z4xzdx]dA=∬D[2zx2]x=0x=zdA=∬D2z(z2−0)dA=∬D2z3dA

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

∬D2z3dA=∫02∫04−2y2z3dzdy=∫02[12z4]z=0z=4−2ydy=∫0212(4−2y))4dy=∫0212(4−2y)2dy=∫0212(16−16y+4y2)dy=∫028−8y+2y2dy=[8y−4y2+23y3]y=0y=2=16−16+163=163

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y}12z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}12z[x]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12z(y-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12yz\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}yz\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-{y}^{2}}12yz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6y[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=4-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6y(4-{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(96y-48{y}^{3}+6{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[48{y}^{2}-12{y}^{4}+{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =48(2)^{2}-12(2)^{4}+(2)^{6} \\  & =64\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∬D[∫0y12zdx]dA=∬D12z[x]x=0x=ydA=∬D12z(y−0)dA=∬D12yzdA

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{y}^{y+z}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{2}]_{x=y}^{x=y+z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+z)^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[y{z}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(16-1) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

∬D[∫01−y−z24ydx]dA=∬D24y[x]x=0x=1−y−zdA=∬D24y(1−y−z)dA=∬D24y−24y2−24yzdA

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Mixed Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} 4x^3 \, \textrm{d}V
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}} 4x^3 \, \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}4{x}^{3}\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{4}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{y}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{(\sqrt{y})}^{4}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/3c8712fa0a30ad94f503efe5e080ee89f83eb21f19fba45033bbedeab08ac816.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{y}^{2}z]_{z=0}^{z=4-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{2}(4-y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}4{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}(64-0)-\frac{1}{4}(256-0) \\  & =\frac{64}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region
question.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 4x^3  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: 0 \leq x \leq \sqrt{y} \right\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the line $z = 4-y$ in the first quadrant.
question.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} 4x^3 \, \textrm{d}V
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}} 4x^3 \, \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}4{x}^{3}\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{4}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{y}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{(\sqrt{y})}^{4}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/3c8712fa0a30ad94f503efe5e080ee89f83eb21f19fba45033bbedeab08ac816.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{y}^{2}z]_{z=0}^{z=4-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{2}(4-y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}4{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}(64-0)-\frac{1}{4}(256-0) \\  & =\frac{64}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}yz[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y+z}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz(y+z)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz({y}^{2}+2yz+{z}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/5974f852ba8dcaf9e6c4d6323709987c590e2f739524e012545738bc4bb842b0.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}\cdot {y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y\cdot {y}^{4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{17}{12}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{17}{72}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 11

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[x]_{x=0}^{x={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/38ea49a6fae41574107b2ba68a578586a306cf43d419d4de5699dcfa009137c2.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{0}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{0}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[({y}^{2}+1)z+\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=-{y}^{2}}^{z=0}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+1)((0-(-{y}^{2}))+\frac{1}{3}(0-{(-{y}^{2})}^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+1){y}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{6}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}+{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{6}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{21}{y}^{7}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{21} \\  & =\frac{61}{105}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=yz}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}(yz)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/acb173db9d28ed8b38e63c7bc365c20e5755aeb1af3f6340e7b9229a4b49101d.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z={y}^{2}}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}({y}^{6}-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{9}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{9}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 14
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}2\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y-z}dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2(4-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-2z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[8z-2yz-{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}8-2y-1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}7-2y\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}7-2y\,dy & ={[7y-{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =7-1 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}2y[x]_{x=0}^{x=z\sqrt{3}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/63a8768b2769fad339ba7667357812d2dda0ea856e846ad666a100f8bc1336e9.png)

$$

tutorial.name: Skipping the Intermediate Step
tutorial.problem:
When writing down a triple integral as a repeated integral, we can often skip the intermediate step of expressing our triple integral as a mixed integral.

For example, suppose we wish to evaluate

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R f(x,y,z)  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type II region given by 

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: {\color{red}a} \leq y \leq {\color{red}b}, \: {\color{blue}v_1(y)} \leq z \leq {\color{blue}v_2(y)}, \: {\color{purple}u_1(y,z)} \leq x \leq {\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} \right\}.
$$

Notice that the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane is a type I plane region. Therefore, we can immediately express our triple integral as a repeated integral as follows:

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{\color{red}a}^{\color{red}b} \int_{\color{blue}v_1(y)}^{\color{blue}v_2(y)} \int_{\color{purple}u_1(y,z)}^{\color{purple}u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/f25c393f10c35ffd9b4fa91cdf672a516cf6cff974a8aa563d350619a64b79bd.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
\iiint \limits_{R}  12z^2  \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{3-y-z}  12z^2  \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=3-y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}(3-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12{z}^{3}-4y{z}^{3}-3{z}^{4}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12-4y-3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy & =[9y-2{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(9-2)-0 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y+2z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/27862dcc3effe5801c812f5c8944c0134d13bb38f99d337b0a4e20e9ff815639.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 4,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y+2z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{z}{12}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y+2z}\frac{z}{12}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{z}{12}[x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y+2z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{z}{12}(4-y+2z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{12}(4z-yz+2{z}^{2})\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}2\,dy & =[2y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =6-0 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Evaluate the triple integral ∭R16−y+3zdV over the region R, shown above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.

e

Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,0≤x≤2−y3+z},

where

D={(y,z):0≤y≤3,0≤z≤3}

is the projection of R onto the yz-plane, shown below.

Hence, we can express the region R as

R={(x,y,z):0≤y≤3,0≤z≤3,0≤2−y3+z}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭R16−y+3zdV=∫03∫03∫02−y/3+z16−y+3zdxdzdy.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∫03∫03∫02−y/3+z16−y+3zdxdzdy=∫03∫03[∫02−y/3+z16−y+3zdx]dzdy=∫03∫0316−y+3z[x]x=0x=2−y/3+zdzdy=∫03∫0316−y+3z(2−y3+z)dzdy=∫03∫0313dzdy

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating y as a constant:

∫03∫0313dzdy=∫03[∫0313dz]dy=∫0313[z]z=0z=3dy=∫0313(3)dy=∫03dy

Finally, we integrate with respect to y:

∫03dy=[y]y=0y=3=3.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/a39d7a27f20283b6e6814db926801f16e3e2cb42c7fe16487350b536d3b63d3c.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-(y-1)^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/5058493860a1c4d919e3cd6786bb1aca156ae83d47f766c087e351e9764929c4.png)

Hence, $D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le 1-(y-1)^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡z[{x}^{2}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1-(y-1)^{2}}3\operatorname{cos}⁡z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Given that R is the type II region shown above, ∭R2xcos⁡zdV=

a
∫02∫01−(y−1)22xsin⁡zdzdy
b
∫02∫013cos⁡zdzdy
c
∫02∫013ycos⁡zdzdy
d
∫02∫013sin⁡zdzdy
e
∫02∫01−(y−1)23cos⁡zdzdy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a type II region R with projection D onto the yz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

We consider the region R as a type II region enclosed between the back surface x=u1(y,z)=1 and the front surface x=u2(y,z)=2.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,1≤x≤2}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type I plane region in the yz-plane with the upper curve

z=1−(y−1)2.

Hence, D={(y,z):0≤y≤2,0≤z≤1−(y−1)2}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭R2xcos⁡zdV=∬D[∫122xcos⁡zdx]dA=∫02∫01−(y−1)2[∫122xcos⁡zdx]dzdy=∫02∫01−(y−1)2cos⁡z[x2]x=1x=2dzdy=∫02∫01−(y−1)23cos⁡zdzdy

observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/2427e053c0e2d808b32db5d7fedf81365e7e50f0b3f2dc61598ad1795394686e.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2+2y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(2+2y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{y}^{2}z+2{y}^{3}z-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{y}^{2}z+2{y}^{3}z-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

Question 20
?

Evaluate the triple integral ∭Ry2dV over the region R, shown above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.

a
2
b
12
c
13
d
1
e
16
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,0≤x≤2+2y−z},

where

D={(y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤1}

is the projection of R onto the yz-plane, shown below.

Hence, we can express the region R as

R={(x,y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤1,0≤x≤2+2y−z}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭Ry2dV=∫01∫01∫02+2y−zy2dxdzdy.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∫01∫01∫02+2y−zy2dxdzdy=∫01∫01[∫02+2y−zy2dx]dzdy=∫01∫01y2[x]x=0x=2+2y−zdzdy=∫01∫01y2(2+2y−z)dzdy=∫01∫012y2+2y3−y2zdzdy

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating y as a constant:

∫01∫012y2+2y3−y2zdzdy=∫01[∫012y2+2y3−y2zdz]dy=∫01[2y2z+2y3z−12y2z2]z=0z=1dy=∫012y2+2y3−12y2dy=∫0132y2+2y3dy

Finally, we integrate with respect to y:

∫0132y2+2y3dy=[12y3+12y4]y=0y=1=(12+12)−0=1.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the type II region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,(3y-z)^{2}\le x\le {e}^{y+4z}\},
$$

where $D$ is some finite region in the $yz$-plane. Then,

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V=
$$
question.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=(3y-z)^{2}\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={e}^{y+4z}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{(3y-z)^{2}}^{{e}^{y+4z}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,(3y−z)2≤x≤ey+4z}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dx]dA
b
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∫(3y−z)2ey+4z[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
d
∫(3y−z)2ey+4z[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dz
e
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=(3y−z)2u2(y,z)=ey+4z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dx]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

last_observation.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=(3y-z)^{2}\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={e}^{y+4z}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{(3y-z)^{2}}^{{e}^{y+4z}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,(3y−z)2≤x≤ey+4z}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dx]dA
b
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∫(3y−z)2ey+4z[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
d
∫(3y−z)2ey+4z[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dz
e
∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=(3y−z)2u2(y,z)=ey+4z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dx]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

solution.reasoning: For each fixed (y,z) in D, x ranges from (3y-z)^2 to e^{y+4z}. Integrate first with respect to x, then integrate over D in the yz-plane. Thus option a is mathematically correct. The supplied worked example supports this rule, but no answer key or grade for the current question is captured.

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,(3y-z)^{2}\le x\le {e}^{y+4z}\},
$$

$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=(3y-z)^{2}\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={e}^{y+4z}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{(3y-z)^{2}}^{{e}^{y+4z}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

b

EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=(3y−z)2u2(y,z)=ey+4z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫(3y−z)2ey+4zf(x,y,z)dx]dA.

question.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-3\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=5{y}^{4}+2.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-3}^{5{y}^{4}+2}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,−3≤x≤5y4+2}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dz
b
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
c
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
d
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA
e
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=−3u2(y,z)=5y4+2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-3\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=5{y}^{4}+2.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-3}^{5{y}^{4}+2}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,−3≤x≤5y4+2}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dz
b
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
c
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
d
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA
e
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=−3u2(y,z)=5y4+2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

solution.reasoning: For each fixed (y,z) in D, integrate with respect to x from -3 to 5y^4+2, then integrate over D in the yz-plane. This gives option d. The supplied example supports the method, but no Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-3\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=5{y}^{4}+2.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-3}^{5{y}^{4}+2}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
The triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz
$$

is defined over the type II region $R,$ given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,-8\le y\le {sin}^{2}⁡z,\,0\le z\le \pi ,\,-2y-1\le x\le {y}^{2}+2z\}.
$$

What is $a+b?$
question.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/a905e1f60fb0aa865c071fcbccbfecb30dcac7a74b4b647d24a40f4c89ff1935.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-2y-1,\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={y}^{2}+2z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-8\le y\le {sin}^{2}⁡z,\,0\le z\le \pi \}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=0+\pi =\pi .
$$

The triple integral ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∫ab∫∗∗∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dxdydz is defined over the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):−8≤y≤sin2⁡z,0≤z≤π,−2y−1≤x≤y2+2z}. What is a+b?

a
sin2⁡z+π−8
b
y2+2z−2y−1
c
sin2⁡z−8
d
π
e
y2+2z−2y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have

u1(y,z)=−2y−1,u2(y,z)=y2+2z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dA.

Now, the region D is given by D={(x,y):−8≤y≤sin2⁡z,0≤z≤π}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get ∬D[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dA=∫0π∫−8sin2⁡z[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dydz=∫0π∫−8sin2⁡z∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dxdydz.

Finally, a+b=0+π=π.

The triple integral ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∫ab∫∗∗∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dxdydz is defined over the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):−z≤y≤1,4≤z≤5,−y+z≤x≤4}. What is a+b?

a
1−z
b
−2
c
4−y+z
d
4+y+z
e
9
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have

u1(y,z)=−y+z,u2(y,z)=4.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−y+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

Now, the region D is given by D={(x,y):−z≤y≤1,4≤z≤5}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get ∬D[∫−y+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dA=∫45∫−z1[∫−y+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dydz=∫45∫−z1∫−y+z4f(x,y,z)dxdydz.

question.html:
Question 5
?

The triple integral ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∫∗∗∫ab∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dxdydz is defined over the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):−2≤y≤z,2≤z≤3,−y−z≤x≤y2+z4}. What is a+b?

a
y2+z4+y+z
b
5
c
y2+z4−y−z
d
z−2
e
z+3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have

u1(y,z)=−y−z,u2(y,z)=y2+z4.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

Now, the region D is given by D={(x,y):−2≤y≤z,2≤z≤3}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get ∬D[∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dA=∫23∫−2z[∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dx]dydz=∫23∫−2z∫−y−zy2+z4f(x,y,z)dxdydz.

Finally, a+b=−2+z=z−2.

solution.reasoning: The middle integral is with respect to y, so a=-2 and b=z. Therefore a+b=z-2, matching option d. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y{z}^{2}}\frac{12}{z}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,1\le z\le \sqrt{2y}\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y{z}^{2}}\frac{12}{z}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{12}{z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=y{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{12}{z}(y{z}^{2}-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12yz\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}12yz\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2y}}12yz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[6y{z}^{2}]_{z=1}^{z=\sqrt{2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6y((\sqrt{2y})^{2}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}6y(2y-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}12{y}^{2}-6y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[4{y}^{3}-3{y}^{2}]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =4(8-1)-3(4-1) \\  & =19\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}4xz\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{4-2y}\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}4xz\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}[2z{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2z({z}^{2}-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2y}}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{4-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{4-2y)})^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(4-2y)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(16-16y+4{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}8-8y+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[8y-4{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =16-16+\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}4xz\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}[2z{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2z({z}^{2}-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2y}}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{4-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{4-2y)})^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(4-2y)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(16-16y+4{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}8-8y+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[8y-4{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =16-16+\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y}12z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le 4-{y}^{2}\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y}12z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}12z[x]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12z(y-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12yz\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}yz\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-{y}^{2}}12yz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6y[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=4-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6y(4-{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(96y-48{y}^{3}+6{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[48{y}^{2}-12{y}^{4}+{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =48(2)^{2}-12(2)^{4}+(2)^{6} \\  & =64\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{y}^{y+z}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le y\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{y}^{y+z}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{2}]_{x=y}^{x=y+z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+z)^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[y{z}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(16-1) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Evaluate the mixed integral ∬D[∫yy+z2xdx]dA where the region D in the yz-plane is given by D={(y,z):1≤y≤2,0≤z≤y}.

a
 12
b
 83
c
 5
d
 53
e
 2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∬D[∫yy+z2xdx]dA=∬D[x2]x=yx=y+zdA=∬D(y+z)2−y2dA=∬D2yz+z2dA

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

∬D2yz+z2dA=∫12∫0y2yz+z2dzdy=∫12[yz2+13z3]z=0z=ydy=∫12y3+13y3dy=∫1243y3dy=[13y4]y=1y=2=13(16−1)=5

last_observation.name: Question 9
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Mixed Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{y}^{y+z}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{2}]_{x=y}^{x=y+z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y+z)^{2}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}2yz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[y{z}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{y=1}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(16-1) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

d

e

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∬D[∫01−y−z24ydx]dA=∬D24y[x]x=0x=1−y−zdA=∬D24y(1−y−z)dA=∬D24y−24y2−24yzdA

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

∬D24y−24y2−24yzdA=∫01/2∫0y24(y−y2)−24yzdzdy=∫01/224(y−y2)[z]z=0z=y−12y[z2]z=0z=ydy=∫01/224(y−y2)y−12y3dy=∫01/224y2−36y3dy=[8y3−9y4]y=0y=1/2=8(18−0)−9(116−0)=716

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le y+z\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the line $z=y$ in the first quadrant.
question.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}yz[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=y+z}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz(y+z)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}yz({y}^{2}+2yz+{z}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/5974f852ba8dcaf9e6c4d6323709987c590e2f739524e012545738bc4bb842b0.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}\cdot {y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y\cdot {y}^{4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{17}{12}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{17}{72}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14216491/assets/5974f852ba8dcaf9e6c4d6323709987c590e2f739524e012545738bc4bb842b0.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{y}{y}^{3}z+2{y}^{2}{z}^{2}+y{z}^{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}{z}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}\cdot {y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{2}\cdot {y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}y\cdot {y}^{4}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{17}{12}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5}\,dy \\  & =\frac{17}{12}{[\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{17}{12}(\frac{1}{6}-0) \\  & =\frac{17}{72}\end{aligned}
$$

where the region R is given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,0≤x≤y+z}, and D is a finite region in yz-plane enclosed between the y-axis, the line y=1 and the line z=y in the first quadrant.

Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain ∭R2xyzdV=∬D[∫0y+z2xyzdx]dA.

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region D in the yz-plane shown below.

Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le y+z\},
$$

feedback.worked_solution:

$$
{∭}_{R}2xyz\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z}2xyz\,dx]dA.
$$

$$
