observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =6xyz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=v} \\  & =6(u)(u+v)(v) \\  & =6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}v}{3}+\frac{{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{v}{3}+\frac{{v}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{[\frac{{v}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{v}^{3}}{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the surface integral ∬S6xyzdS, where the parametric surface S is defined by r(u,v)=⟨u,u+v,v⟩ over the domain D={(u,v):0≤u≤1,0≤v≤1}.

Hint: You can use the fact that ‖ru′×rv′‖=3.

EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

‖ru′×rv′‖=3.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=6xyz|x=uy=u+vz=v=6(u)(u+v)(v)=6(u2v+uv2)

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D6(u2v+uv2)⋅3dA=63∬D(u2v+uv2)dA=63∫01(∫01(u2v+uv2)du)dv=63∫01[u3v3+u2v22]01dv=63∫01(v3+v22)dv=63[v26+v36]01=63(16+16)=23.

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{2}{3}v+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 8

observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3x-2y+3z)\,{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u+v\,z=-v} \\  & =3(2u+v)-2(2u+v)+3(-v) \\  & =2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2(u-v)\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,(u-v)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}({\int }_{-1}^{1}u-v\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-vu]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(0-2v)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-{v}^{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =2xz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-3,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-8)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+64+36} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =x(y+z)\,{|}_{x=2u\,y=-3v\,z=4v} \\  & =2u(-3v+4v) \\  & =2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}x(y+z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2uv\cdot 10\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =5\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =5\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Evaluate the surface integral ∬Sx(y+z)dS, where the parametric surface S is defined by the equations x=2u,y=−3v,z=4v for 0≤u≤2 and 0≤v≤2.

a
95
b
80
c
85
d
75
e
90
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

In vector form, our surface has the equation

r(u,v)=⟨2u,−3v,4v⟩.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(2u),∂∂u(−3v),∂∂u(4v)⟩=⟨2,0,0⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(2u),∂∂v(−3v),∂∂v(4v)⟩=⟨0,−3,4⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk2000−34|=⟨|00−34|,−|2004|,|200−3|⟩=⟨0,−8,−6⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨0,−8,−6⟩‖=02+(−8)2+(−6)2=0+64+36=100=10.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=x(y+z)|x=2uy=−3vz=4v=2u(−3v+4v)=2uv

Therefore, if we denote

D={(u,v):0≤u≤2,0≤v≤2},

our surface integral can be written as

∬Sx(y+z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D2uv⋅10dA=5∬D4uvdA=5∫022udu⋅∫022vdv=5⋅[u2]02⋅[v2]02=5⋅4⋅4=80.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=x+z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨uv,\,{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}.$*
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(x+z)\,{|}_{x=uv\,y={u}^{2}\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =uv+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(uv+{v}^{2})\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=x+z over the parametric surface r(u,v)=⟨uv,u2,v2⟩ for (u,v)∈D⊆R2. What is the missing expression?

Hint: You can use the fact that ‖ru′×rv′‖=16u2v2+4v4+4u4.

a
v2u2v2+4v4+4u4
b
(uv+u2)16u2v2+4v2+4u4
c
(uv+v2)16u2v2+4v4+4u4
d
uvu2v2+4v4+4u4
e
(v+v2)16u2v2+4v2+4u4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

‖ru′×rv′‖=16u2v2+4v4+4u4.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(x+z)|x=uvy=u2z=v2=uv+v2

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(uv+v2)16u2v2+4v4+4u4dA.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(x+z)\,{|}_{x=uv\,y={u}^{2}\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =uv+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(uv+{v}^{2})\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=x+z over the parametric surface r(u,v)=⟨uv,u2,v2⟩ for (u,v)∈D⊆R2. What is the missing expression?

Hint: You can use the fact that ‖ru′×rv′‖=16u2v2+4v4+4u4.

a
v2u2v2+4v4+4u4
b
(uv+u2)16u2v2+4v2+4u4
c
(uv+v2)16u2v2+4v4+4u4
d
uvu2v2+4v4+4u4
e
(v+v2)16u2v2+4v2+4u4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

‖ru′×rv′‖=16u2v2+4v4+4u4.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(x+z)|x=uvy=u2z=v2=uv+v2

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(uv+v2)16u2v2+4v4+4u4dA.
question.knowledge_point: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

solution.reasoning: For a scalar surface integral, the integrand is f(r(u,v))‖r_u×r_v‖. Substituting x=uv and z=v² gives f(r(u,v))=uv+v². Multiplying by the supplied surface-area factor gives option c. The captured worked solution concerns a different example, so it does not establish Math Academy's answer key for this question.

feedback.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=x+z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨uv,\,{u}^{2},\,{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(x+z)\,{|}_{x=uv\,y={u}^{2}\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =uv+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(uv+{v}^{2})\sqrt{16{u}^{2}{v}^{2}+4{v}^{4}+4{u}^{4}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

r(u,v)=⟨u,\,{v}^{2}-{u}^{2},\,u⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2u,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2u & 1 \\ 0 & 2v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-2u & 1 \\ 2v & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & -2u \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u,\,0,\,2v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-2v,\,0,\,2v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-2v)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+4{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-y-z)\,{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}-{u}^{2}\,z=u} \\  & =-u-({v}^{2}-{u}^{2})-u \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u)\sqrt{8}v\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=−x−y−z over the parametric surface r(u,v)=⟨u,v2−u2,u⟩ for (u,v)∈D⊆R2. What is the missing expression?

a
(v2−u2−2)8
b
(u2−v2)8u
c
(u2+2v+2u)8v
d
(u2+v2+u)8v
e
(u2−v2−2u)8v
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u),∂∂u(v2−u2),∂∂u(u)⟩=⟨1,−2u,1⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u),∂∂v(v2−u2),∂∂v(u)⟩=⟨0,2v,0⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk1−2u102v0|=⟨|−2u12v0|,−|1100|,|1−2u02v|⟩=⟨−2u,0,2v⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨−2v,0,2v⟩‖=(−2v)2+(0)2+(2v)2=4v2+4v2=8v.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(−x−y−z)|x=uy=v2−u2z=u=−u−(v2−u2)−u=u2−v2−2u

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(u2−v2−2u)8vdA.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2u,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2u & 1 \\ 0 & 2v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-2u & 1 \\ 2v & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & -2u \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u,\,0,\,2v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-2v,\,0,\,2v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-2v)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+4{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-y-z)\,{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}-{u}^{2}\,z=u} \\  & =-u-({v}^{2}-{u}^{2})-u \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u)\sqrt{8}v\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=-x-y-z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,{v}^{2}-{u}^{2},\,u⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?

EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u),∂∂u(v2−u2),∂∂u(u)⟩=⟨1,−2u,1⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u),∂∂v(v2−u2),∂∂v(u)⟩=⟨0,2v,0⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk1−2u102v0|=⟨|−2u12v0|,−|1100|,|1−2u02v|⟩=⟨−2u,0,2v⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨−2v,0,2v⟩‖=(−2v)2+(0)2+(2v)2=4v2+4v2=8v.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(−x−y−z)|x=uy=v2−u2z=u=−u−(v2−u2)−u=u2−v2−2u

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(u2−v2−2u)8vdA.

feedback.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=-x-y-z$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,{v}^{2}-{u}^{2},\,u⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2u,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}-{u}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2u & 1 \\ 0 & 2v & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}-2u & 1 \\ 2v & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & -2u \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2u,\,0,\,2v⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-2v,\,0,\,2v⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-2v)^{2}+(0)^{2}+(2v)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+4{v}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-y-z)\,{|}_{x=u\,y={v}^{2}-{u}^{2}\,z=u} \\  & =-u-({v}^{2}-{u}^{2})-u \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}-{v}^{2}-2u)\sqrt{8}v\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

a
(v2−u2−2)8

EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u),∂∂u(v2−u2),∂∂u(u)⟩=⟨1,−2u,1⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u),∂∂v(v2−u2),∂∂v(u)⟩=⟨0,2v,0⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk1−2u102v0|=⟨|−2u12v0|,−|1100|,|1−2u02v|⟩=⟨−2u,0,2v⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨−2v,0,2v⟩‖=(−2v)2+(0)2+(2v)2=4v2+4v2=8v.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(−x−y−z)|x=uy=v2−u2z=u=−u−(v2−u2)−u=u2−v2−2u

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(u2−v2−2u)8vdA.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=xyz$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,uv⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v \\ 1 & u\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-v)^{2}+(-u)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(xyz)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=uv} \\  & =u\cdot v\cdot uv \\  & ={u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u),∂∂u(v),∂∂u(uv)⟩=⟨1,0,v⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u),∂∂v(v),∂∂v(uv)⟩=⟨0,1,u⟩

and

last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v \\ 1 & u\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-v)^{2}+(-u)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(xyz)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=uv} \\  & =u\cdot v\cdot uv \\  & ={u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=xyz over the parametric surface r(u,v)=⟨u,v,uv⟩ for (u,v)∈D⊆R2. What is the missing expression?

a
u2v2u+v
b
uvu2+v2+1
c
u2v2u2+v2+1
d
uvuv
e
u2v2uv
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u),∂∂u(v),∂∂u(uv)⟩=⟨1,0,v⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u),∂∂v(v),∂∂v(uv)⟩=⟨0,1,u⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk10v01u|=⟨|0v1u|,−|1v0u|,|1001|⟩=⟨−v,−u,1⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨−v,−u,1⟩‖=(−v)2+(−u)2+(1)2=u2+v2+1.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(xyz)|x=uy=vz=uv=u⋅v⋅uv=u2v2

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬Du2v2u2+v2+1dA.
question.knowledge_point: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

solution.reasoning: Substitution gives f(r(u,v))=u·v·uv=u²v². The tangent vectors are r_u=(1,0,v) and r_v=(0,1,u), so r_u×r_v=(−v,−u,1), whose norm is √(u²+v²+1). Their product is option c. feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=xyz$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,uv⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,v⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(uv)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & v \\ 0 & 1 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & v \\ 1 & u\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & v \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨-v,\,-u,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-v)^{2}+(-u)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(xyz)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=v\,z=uv} \\  & =u\cdot v\cdot uv \\  & ={u}^{2}{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}{v}^{2}\sqrt{{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=xz+y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,-v,\,-{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}.$*
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(xz+y)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=-v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =u\cdot (-{v}^{2})+(-v) \\  & =-u{v}^{2}-v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(-u{v}^{2}-v)\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: You can use the fact that ‖ru′×rv′‖=1+4v2.

EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

‖ru′×rv′‖=1+4v2.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(xz+y)|x=uy=−vz=v2=u⋅(−v2)+(−v)=−uv2−v

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(−uv2−v)1+4v2dA.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(xz+y)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=-v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =u\cdot (-{v}^{2})+(-v) \\  & =-u{v}^{2}-v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(-u{v}^{2}-v)\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=xz+y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,-v,\,-{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}.$*

Question 4

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=xz+y over the parametric surface r(u,v)=⟨u,−v,−v2⟩ for (u,v)∈D⊆R2. What is the missing expression?

Hint: You can use the fact that ‖ru′×rv′‖=1+4v2.

a
(−uv−v)1+4v2
b
(−uv2+v2)1+4v2
c
(−uv2−v)1+4v2
d
(−uv2+v)1+4v2
e
(uv2−v2)1+4v2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

‖ru′×rv′‖=1+4v2.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(xz+y)|x=uy=−vz=v2=u⋅(−v2)+(−v)=−uv2−v

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(−uv2−v)1+4v2dA.

solution.reasoning: Substituting x=u, y=−v, and z=−v² gives f(r(u,v))=−uv²−v. Multiplying by the surface-area factor √(1+4v²) yields option c. The supplied worked solution is for a different example, so Math Academy's key for this question is not captured.

feedback.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=xz+y$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,-v,\,-{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(xz+y)\,{|}_{x=u\,y=-v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =u\cdot (-{v}^{2})+(-v) \\  & =-u{v}^{2}-v\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(-u{v}^{2}-v)\sqrt{1+4{v}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=xz+y over the parametric surface r(u,v)=⟨u,−v,−v2⟩ for (u,v)∈D⊆R2. What is the missing expression?

Hint: You can use the fact that ‖ru′×rv′‖=1+4v2.

a
(−uv−v)1+4v2
b
(−uv2+v2)1+4v2
c
(−uv2−v)1+4v2
d
(−uv2+v)1+4v2
e
(uv2−v2)1+4v2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product for our surface is

‖ru′×rv′‖=1+4v2.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(xz+y)|x=uy=−vz=v2=u⋅(−v2)+(−v)=−uv2−v

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D(−uv2−v)1+4v2dA.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=-x-{z}^{2}$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{3},\,v,\,{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3{u}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-6v{u}^{2})^{2}+(3{u}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{v}^{2}{u}^{4}+9{u}^{4}} \\  & =3{u}^{2}\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x={u}^{3}\,y=v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =-{u}^{3}-({v}^{2}\cdot {v}^{2}) \\  & =-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,3{u}^{2}(-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4})\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3{u}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-6v{u}^{2})^{2}+(3{u}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{v}^{2}{u}^{4}+9{u}^{4}} \\  & =3{u}^{2}\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x={u}^{3}\,y=v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =-{u}^{3}-({v}^{2}\cdot {v}^{2}) \\  & =-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,3{u}^{2}(-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4})\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=−x−z2 over the parametric surface r(u,v)=⟨u3,v,v2⟩ for (u,v)∈D⊆R2. What is the missing expression?

a
u(−u3−v4)4v3+u
b
6v2(u2+v4)v2+1
c
u2(−u3+v4)4uv+u
d
3u2(−u3−v4)4v2+1
e
3u2(u4−v3)4u2+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u3),∂∂u(v),∂∂u(v2)⟩=⟨3u2,0,0⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u3),∂∂v(v),∂∂v(v2)⟩=⟨0,1,2v⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk3u200012v|=⟨|0012v|,−|3u2002v|,|3u2001|⟩=⟨0,−6vu2,3u2⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨0,−6vu2,3u2⟩‖=(0)2+(−6vu2)2+(3u2)2=36v2u4+9u4=3u24v2+1.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=(−x−z2)|x=u3y=vz=v2=−u3−(v2⋅v2)=−u3−v4

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D3u2(−u3−v4)4v2+1dA.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

Consider the surface integral of the function 
$f(x,y,z)=-x-{z}^{2}$ 
over the parametric surface 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨{u}^{3},\,v,\,{v}^{2}⟩
$$

for $(u,v)\in D⊆{R}^{2}.$ What is the missing expression?
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{u}^{2},\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{3}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3{u}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2v\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}3{u}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-6v{u}^{2},\,3{u}^{2}⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(-6v{u}^{2})^{2}+(3{u}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{v}^{2}{u}^{4}+9{u}^{4}} \\  & =3{u}^{2}\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(-x-{z}^{2})\,{|}_{x={u}^{3}\,y=v\,z={v}^{2}} \\  & =-{u}^{3}-({v}^{2}\cdot {v}^{2}) \\  & =-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,3{u}^{2}(-{u}^{3}-{v}^{4})\sqrt{4{v}^{2}+1}\,\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(u3),∂∂u(v),∂∂u(v2)⟩=⟨3u2,0,0⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(u3),∂∂v(v),∂∂v(v2)⟩=⟨0,1,2v⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk3u200012v|=⟨|0012v|,−|3u2002v|,|3u2001|⟩=⟨0,−6vu2,3u2⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨0,−6vu2,3u2⟩‖=(0)2+(−6vu2)2+(3u2)2=36v2u4+9u4=3u24v2+1.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}6xyz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,v⟩
$$

 
over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.$*
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =6xyz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=v} \\  & =6(u)(u+v)(v) \\  & =6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}v}{3}+\frac{{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{v}{3}+\frac{{v}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{[\frac{{v}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{v}^{3}}{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Evaluate the surface integral ∬S6xyzdS, where the parametric surface S is defined by r(u,v)=⟨u,u+v,v⟩ over the domain D={(u,v):0≤u≤1,0≤v≤1}.

Hint: You can use the fact that ‖ru′×rv′‖=3.

a
23
b
3
c
34
d
43
e
33
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

‖ru′×rv′‖=3.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=6xyz|x=uy=u+vz=v=6(u)(u+v)(v)=6(u2v+uv2)

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D6(u2v+uv2)⋅3dA=63∬D(u2v+uv2)dA=63∫01(∫01(u2v+uv2)du)dv=63∫01[u3v3+u2v22]01dv=63∫01(v3+v22)dv=63[v26+v36]01=63(16+16)=23.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =6xyz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=v} \\  & =6(u)(u+v)(v) \\  & =6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,6({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}v+u{v}^{2})\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}v}{3}+\frac{{u}^{2}{v}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{v}{3}+\frac{{v}^{2}}{2})\,\text{d}v \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{[\frac{{v}^{2}}{6}+\frac{{v}^{3}}{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u+v,\,y=u,\,z=v
$$

for $-1\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 1.$
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{2}{3}v+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

r(u,v)=⟨u+v,u,v⟩.

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨1,−1,−1⟩‖=12+−12+−12=1+1+1=3.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,u,\,v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}+-{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & ={x}^{2}-2yz\,{|}_{x=u+v\,y=u\,z=v} \\  & =(u+v)^{2}-2uv \\  & ={u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{x}^{2}-2yz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,({u}^{2}+{v}^{2})\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}+{v}^{2}\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+u{v}^{2}]}_{u=-1}^{u=1}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{2}{3}+2{v}^{2}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{2}{3}v+\frac{2}{3}{v}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(3x-2y+3z)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u+v,\,2u+v,\,-v⟩
$$

 
over the domain $D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,-1\le v\le 0\}.$

*Hint: You can use the fact that $‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.$*
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

Notice that we are told that the norm of the fundamental vector product is

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3x-2y+3z)\,{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u+v\,z=-v} \\  & =3(2u+v)-2(2u+v)+3(-v) \\  & =2(u-v)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2(u-v)\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,(u-v)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}({\int }_{-1}^{1}u-v\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-vu]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(0-2v)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-{v}^{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖=2\sqrt{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =(3x-2y+3z)\,{|}_{x=2u+v\,y=2u+v\,z=-v} \\  & =3(2u+v)-2(2u+v)+3(-v) \\  & =2(u-v)\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2(u-v)\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{∬}_{D}\,(u-v)\,\text{d}A \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}({\int }_{-1}^{1}u-v\,\text{d}u)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}-vu]}_{-1}^{1}\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(0-2v)\text{d}v \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-{v}^{2}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=u,\,y=u+v,\,z=2v
$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =2xz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}

last_observation.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u+v,\,2v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+1} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =2xz\,{|}_{x=u\,y=u+v\,z=2v} \\  & =2u(2v) \\  & =4uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}2xz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4uv\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =3\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =3\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}x(y+z)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=2u,\,y=-3v,\,z=4v
$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$
question.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u,\,-3v,\,4v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-3,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-8)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+64+36} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =x(y+z)\,{|}_{x=2u\,y=-3v\,z=4v} \\  & =2u(-3v+4v) \\  & =2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}x(y+z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2uv\cdot 10\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =5\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =5\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Evaluate the surface integral ∬Sx(y+z)dS, where the parametric surface S is defined by the equations x=2u,y=−3v,z=4v for 0≤u≤2 and 0≤v≤2.

a
95
b
80
c
85
d
75
e
90
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA.

In vector form, our surface has the equation

r(u,v)=⟨2u,−3v,4v⟩.

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

ru′=⟨∂x∂u,∂y∂u,∂z∂u⟩=⟨∂∂u(2u),∂∂u(−3v),∂∂u(4v)⟩=⟨2,0,0⟩rv′=⟨∂x∂v,∂y∂v,∂z∂v⟩=⟨∂∂v(2u),∂∂v(−3v),∂∂v(4v)⟩=⟨0,−3,4⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is ru′×rv′=|ijk2000−34|=⟨|00−34|,−|2004|,|200−3|⟩=⟨0,−8,−6⟩,

and

‖ru′×rv′‖=‖⟨0,−8,−6⟩‖=02+(−8)2+(−6)2=0+64+36=100=10.

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of r(u,v) into f(x,y,z):

f(r(u,v))=x(y+z)|x=2uy=−3vz=4v=2u(−3v+4v)=2uv

Therefore, if we denote

D={(u,v):0≤u≤2,0≤v≤2},

our surface integral can be written as

∬Sx(y+z)dS=∬Df(r(u,v))‖ru′×rv′‖dA=∬D2uv⋅10dA=5∬D4uvdA=5∫022udu⋅∫022vdv=5⋅[u2]02⋅[v2]02=5⋅4⋅4=80.
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating Surface Integrals Over Parametric Surfaces

solution.reasoning: Substitution gives x(y+z)=2u(−3v+4v)=2uv. The tangent vectors (2,0,0) and (0,−3,4) have cross product (0,−8,−6), with norm 10. Therefore the integral is 20(∫₀²u du)(∫₀²v dv)=20·2·2=80, option b. No captured answer or grade establishes Math Academy's key for this question.

feedback.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}x(y+z)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where the parametric surface $S$ is defined by the equations

$$
x=2u,\,y=-3v,\,z=4v
$$

for $0\le u\le 2$ and $0\le v\le 2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

In vector form, our surface has the equation 

$$
r(u,v)=⟨2u,\,-3v,\,4v⟩.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-3v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-3,\,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨0,\,-8,\,-6⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-8)^{2}+(-6)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+64+36} \\  & =\sqrt{100} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(u,v)) & =x(y+z)\,{|}_{x=2u\,y=-3v\,z=4v} \\  & =2u(-3v+4v) \\  & =2uv\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if we denote 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 2\},
$$

our surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}x(y+z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(r(u,v))‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2uv\cdot 10\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,4uv\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{2}2u\,\text{d}u\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2v\,\text{d}v \\  & =5\cdot [{u}^{2}]_{0}^{2}\cdot [{v}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =5\cdot 4\cdot 4 \\  & =80.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{2}+8t,\,y=4{t}^{7},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+3t,\,y=1+\sqrt{2t},\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=2$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=2$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(0,\,\frac{16}{7})$ is the $y$-intercept.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{5}-4{t}^{3},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent line is $y=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(-2,1).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the Cartesian equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope $m=-1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =-(x+2) \\ y & =-x-2+1 \\ y & =-x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the tangent line  in slope-intercept form is $y=-x-1.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\sqrt{t+1},\,y={t}^{3}+4,\,-1<t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2}, \\ y & =(1)^{3}+4=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},5).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}})} \\  & =6{t}^{2}\sqrt{(t+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =6\cdot {1}^{2}\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\sqrt{2},5)$ and the slope $m=6\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5 & =6\sqrt{2}(x-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}t+\frac{3}{2},\,y={t}^{3}+7{t}^{2}+8t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=-1$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)+\frac{3}{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+7(-1)^{2}+8(-1)=-1+7-8=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,-2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}+14t+8}{2t+\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}+14(-1)+8}{2(-1)+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,-2)$ and the slope $m=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =2(x-2) \\ y+2 & =2x-4 \\ y & =2x-4-2 \\ y & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)-6 \\ y & =0-6 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-6).$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2(t+1),\,y=4{t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is horizontal.
questions.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is horizontal if ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2,\,{y}^{′}(t)=8t.
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
8t=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Note that ${x}^{′}(0)=2\ne 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that when $t=0,$ the tangent to the curve is horizontal.

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)),\,{y}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =0 \\ 0 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)} & =1 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)=1 \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})]=\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}\ne 0, \\ {y}^{′}(\frac{5\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{5\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})]=-\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{5\pi }{4}}\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $t=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{5}-4{t}^{3},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=1$ on the curve. Find the Cartesian equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$

The Cartesian equation of the normal line at $C$ is $y=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(-2,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-1)\,}=1
$$

Finally, to find the Cartesian equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =x+2 \\ y & =x+2+1 \\ y & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the normal line  in slope-intercept form is $y=x+3.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi }),\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\pi $ on the curve. Determine the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\pi $ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-\pi )$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-\pi ) & =4(x-0) \\ y & =4x-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The normal intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\pi  & =0 \\ 4x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ is the $x$-intercept.
