questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,y=2t\operatorname{ln}⁡t,\,0<t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=e$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=e$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡e=4, \\ y & =2e\operatorname{ln}⁡e=2e\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(4,2e).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{4}{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t+2}{(\frac{4}{t})} \\  & =\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡t+t}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=e,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=e} & =\frac{e\operatorname{ln}⁡e+e}{2} \\  & =\frac{e+e}{2}=e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(4,2e)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{\,e\,}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2e & =(-\frac{1}{\,e\,})(x-4) \\ y-2e & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{4}{\,e\,} \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\,e\,}x+\frac{2{e}^{2}+4}{\,e\,}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0<t<2\pi .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,\frac{\pi }{6}} & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{3(3)}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,y=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,,\,t\in (0,\pi ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})]=\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0, \\ y & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(0,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$  the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /2} & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-1)\,}=1
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1\cdot (x-0) \\ y & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=1-{e}^{3t},\,y=4{t}^{3},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the value of the parameter $t$ at which the normal line to the curve is vertical.
questions.worked_solution:
The normal line is vertical when the tangent to the curve is horizontal. Therefore, we require ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3{e}^{3t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=12{t}^{2}
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
12{t}^{2}=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(0)=-3{e}^{3(0)}=-3\ne 0,\,\,
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=0.$

questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{4}+2{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-3t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .

Determine the value of the parameter $t$ at which the normal line to the curve is horizontal.
questions.worked_solution:
The normal line is horizontal when the tangent line to the curve is vertical. Therefore, we require ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4{t}^{3}+4t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}-3
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
4t({t}^{2}+1)=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
{y}^{′}(0)=3(0)^{2}-3=-3\ne 0,
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when $t=0.$

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+5,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+4,\,0\le t<\pi .
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the normal to the curve is horizontal.
questions.worked_solution:
The normal is horizontal if the tangent is vertical. Therefore, we require ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
-8\operatorname{sin}⁡2t=0\,⟹\,t=0,\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=10\ne 0, \\ {y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =10\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-10\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when $t=0$ and $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=7(t-1),\,y=2{t}^{3}-18t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the points at which the normal to the curve is vertical.
questions.worked_solution:
The normal is vertical if the tangent is horizontal. Therefore, we require ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=7,\,{y}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2}-18.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
6({t}^{2}-3)=0\,⟹\,t=\pm \sqrt{3}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(-\sqrt{3}) & =7\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) & =7\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=\pm \sqrt{3}.$

questions.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{-t},\,y=5{t}^{2}+1,\,0\le t\le 2.
$$

Determine the value of the parameter $t$ at which the normal line to the curve is vertical.
questions.worked_solution:
The normal line is vertical when the tangent to the curve is horizontal. Therefore, we require ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-{e}^{-t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=10t
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
10t=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(0)=-{e}^{-0}=-1\ne 0,\,\,
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=0.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
Suppose that we have a curve defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2t+3, \quad y=t^3-4t, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty.
$$

What is the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $t=-1?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(-1)+3=1, \\ y & =(-1)^{3}-4(-1)=-1+4=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(1,3).$ The plot below shows the curve and the tangent line at this point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217746/assets/0fa3fc12e83e2a581499680145df9229917c7426e6a3d12c51d88e115a42033e.png)

To find the slope of the tangent line, we need to find $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t) = 2, \qquad y'(t) = 3t^2-4 .
$$

So, we have

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)} = \dfrac{3t^2-4}{2}.
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}-4}{2}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $(x_1,y_1) = (1,3)$ and the slope $m=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
y - 3 = -\frac{1}{2}\left(x-1\right).
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Points Where the Tangent is Horizontal or Vertical
canonical_examples.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=t^2+3, \quad y=-t+1, \qquad -\infty <     t <    \infty.
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t) \neq 0 .$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
x'(t) = 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -1 .
$$

Solving $x'(t) = 0$ gives

$$
2t=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=0.
$$

Note that $y'(0) = -1\neq 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that when $t = 0,$ the tangent to the curve is vertical.

Example: 
                    Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217746/assets/9dcc4c97bd296ef4627b02b6cfafcdb643f475cd8dacd36a820db760bd6fb045.png)

The following parametric equations define the curve shown above:

$$
x=2\cos{t} +\sin{2t},\quad y=\cos{t} - 2\sin{2t},\qquad 0\leq t<2\pi
$$

Calculate the equation of the normal to the curve at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (shown as a dashed line in the plot above).
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}+1, \\  \\ y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2(1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $\left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right).$ For this, we need to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t) = -2\sin t + 2\cos 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -\sin t - 4 \cos 2t .
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))} \\  & =-\frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}+4(0)}{2(0-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope $m_n$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = -2
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the normal line, we use the point-slope form 

$$
y - y_1 = m_n(x-x_1),
$$

with

$$
(x_1,y_1) = \left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right), \qquad m_n=-2,
$$

and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2) & =-2(x-(\sqrt{2}+1)) \\ y-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+2 & =-2x+2\sqrt{2}+2 \\ y+2x & =\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Points Where the Normal is Horizontal or Vertical
canonical_examples.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2t^3-1,\quad y=t^2-t+1,\qquad-\infty < t <\infty.
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the **normal** to the curve is horizontal.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The normal is horizontal if the tangent is vertical. Therefore, we require $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t) \neq 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving $x'(t) = 0$ gives

$$
6t^2 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t = 0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2\cdot 0-1=-1\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when $t = 0.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Remember that to find the slope $m$ of a tangent line to a function $y=f(x),$ we compute the derivative:

$$
m = \dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = f'(x)
$$

Likewise, to find the slope $m_n$ of a normal line to a function $y=f(x),$ we take the negative reciprocal of the tangent slope:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{1}{f'(x)}
$$

With parametric equations $x=x(t), \, y=y(t),$ it works the same way. The slope of the tangent line is still the derivative of $y$ with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
m = \dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm dx} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}
$$

Likewise, the slope of the normal line is still given by the negative reciprocal:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{x'(t)}{y'(t)}
$$

tutorials.name: Horizontal or Vertical Tangents to Parametric Curves
tutorials.problem:
The slope $m$ of the tangent to a parametric curve $x=x(t), y=y(t),$ is given by

$$
m = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Suppose that we want to find all of the locations where the tangent to the curve is horizontal. If the tangent is horizontal, this means that $m=0,$ and so provided that $x'(t)\neq 0,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)} = 0\quad \Longrightarrow\quad y'(t) = 0.
$$

So, to find the locations where the tangent is horizontal, we solve the equation $y'(t) = 0.$ We also need to double-check that $x'(t)\neq 0$ for each solution. The final step is necessary because a slope of $\dfrac00$ is meaningless, and we cannot deduce any information regarding the tangent slope from this expression.

Similarly, if we want to find the locations where the tangent line is *vertical,* we solve the equation $x'(t)=0,$ and we also need to check that $y'(t)\neq 0$ for each solution.

Let's see some examples.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=2t2+8t,y=4t7,−∞<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−2=7(x−10)
b
y−4=143(x−3)
c
y+2=76(x−10)
d
y−4=73(x−10)
e
y+4=37(x−10)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=2(1)2+8(1)=2+8=10,y=4(1)7=4.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (10,4).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=4t+8,y′(t)=28t6.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=28t64t+8.

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=28⋅(1)64⋅(1)+8=73.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(10,4) and the slope m=73. We get y−4=73(x−10).

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=2$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(0,\,\frac{16}{7})$ is the $y$-intercept.

$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=2$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis.

$$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

question.html:
Question 2
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t2+3t,y=1+2t,t∈[0,∞). Let C be the point that corresponds to t=2 on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at C crosses the y-axis.

a
(0,−57)
b
(0,167)
c
(0,−27)
d
(0,127)
e
(0,165)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=2 into the parametric equations: x=(2)2+3(2)=10,y=1+2(2)=3.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point (10,3).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=2t+3,y′(t)=12t.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=12t2t+3=12t(2t+3).

At the point where t=2, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=2=12⋅2(2⋅2+3)=114.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(10,3) and the slope m=114. We get y−3=114(x−10).

The tangent crosses the y-axis when x=0. At this point, we have

y−3=114(0−10)y−3=−57y=167.

Consequently, (0,167) is the y-intercept.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(-2,1).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the Cartesian equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope $m=-1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =-(x+2) \\ y & =-x-2+1 \\ y & =-x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the tangent line  in slope-intercept form is $y=-x-1.$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2}, \\ y & =(1)^{3}+4=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},5).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}})} \\  & =6{t}^{2}\sqrt{(t+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =6\cdot {1}^{2}\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\sqrt{2},5)$ and the slope $m=6\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5 & =6\sqrt{2}(x-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t+1,y=t3+4,−1<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−5=62(x−2)
b
y+2=324(x+5)
c
y+5=23(x+2)
d
y−5=2(x−2)
e
y−5=6(x−2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=1+1=2,y=(1)3+4=5.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (2,5).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=12t+1,y′(t)=3t2.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=3t2(12t+1)=6t2(t+1).

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=6⋅121+1=62.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(2,5) and the slope m=62. We get y−5=62(x−2).

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)+\frac{3}{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+7(-1)^{2}+8(-1)=-1+7-8=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,-2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}+14t+8}{2t+\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}+14(-1)+8}{2(-1)+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,-2)$ and the slope $m=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =2(x-2) \\ y+2 & =2x-4 \\ y & =2x-4-2 \\ y & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)-6 \\ y & =0-6 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-6).$

tutorial.name: Horizontal or Vertical Tangents to Parametric Curves
tutorial.problem:
The slope $m$ of the tangent to a parametric curve $x=x(t), y=y(t),$ is given by

$$
m = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Suppose that we want to find all of the locations where the tangent to the curve is horizontal. If the tangent is horizontal, this means that $m=0,$ and so provided that $x'(t)\neq 0,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)} = 0\quad \Longrightarrow\quad y'(t) = 0.
$$

So, to find the locations where the tangent is horizontal, we solve the equation $y'(t) = 0.$ We also need to double-check that $x'(t)\neq 0$ for each solution. The final step is necessary because a slope of $\dfrac00$ is meaningless, and we cannot deduce any information regarding the tangent slope from this expression.

Similarly, if we want to find the locations where the tangent line is *vertical,* we solve the equation $x'(t)=0,$ and we also need to check that $y'(t)\neq 0$ for each solution.

Let's see some examples.

observed_steps.name: Example: Determining the Points Where the Tangent is Horizontal or Vertical
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t) \neq 0 .$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
x'(t) = 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -1 .
$$

Solving $x'(t) = 0$ gives

$$
2t=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t=0.
$$

Note that $y'(0) = -1\neq 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that when $t = 0,$ the tangent to the curve is vertical.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}+1, \\  \\ y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2(1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $\left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right).$ For this, we need to find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
x'(t) = -2\sin t + 2\cos 2t, \qquad y'(t) = -\sin t - 4 \cos 2t .
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}))} \\  & =-\frac{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}+4(0)}{2(0-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope $m_n$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
m_n = -\dfrac{1}{m} = -\dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = -2
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the normal line, we use the point-slope form 

$$
y - y_1 = m_n(x-x_1),
$$

with

$$
(x_1,y_1) = \left(\sqrt{2}+1,\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} -2\right), \qquad m_n=-2,
$$

and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-2) & =-2(x-(\sqrt{2}+1)) \\ y-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+2 & =-2x+2\sqrt{2}+2 \\ y+2x & =\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\pi $ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-\pi )$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-\pi ) & =4(x-0) \\ y & =4x-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The normal intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\pi  & =0 \\ 4x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ is the $x$-intercept.

question.html:
Question 13
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=4ln⁡t,y=2tln⁡t,0<t<∞. Let C be the point that corresponds to t=e on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at C.

a
y=−1ex+2e2+4e
b
y=1ex+2e2−4e
c
y=−4ex+2e2−4e
d
y=2ex+4e2−2e
e
y=2ex−2e2−4e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=e into the parametric equations: x=4ln⁡e=4,y=2eln⁡e=2e So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point (4,2e). For this, we need to find dydx, which means we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=4t,y′(t)=2ln⁡t+2

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=2ln⁡t+2(4t)=tln⁡t+t2.

At the point where t=e, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=e=eln⁡e+e2=e+e2=e.

To find the slope mn of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of m:

mn=−1m=−1e

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(4,2e) and the slope mn=−1e. We get

y−2e=(−1e)(x−4)y−2e=−1ex+4ey=−1ex+2e2+4e.
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve

observed_steps.name: Question 14
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{6},$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,\frac{\pi }{6}} & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{3}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=\sqrt{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ y-\frac{1}{2} & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{3(3)}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-\frac{9}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt{3}x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$

The normal crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-4).$

observed_steps.name: Question 15
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})]=\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0, \\ y & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(0,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$  the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi /2} & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-1)\,}=1
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1\cdot (x-0) \\ y & =x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=ln⁡(sin⁡t),y=1sin⁡t,t∈(0,π). Let C be the point that corresponds to t=π2 on the curve. Find the equation of the normal to the curve at C.

a
y=2x+1
b
y=2x+3
c
y=x+1
d
y=x+2
e
y=x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=π2 into the parametric equations: x=ln⁡[sin⁡(π2)]=ln⁡1=0,y=1sin⁡(π2)=1

So we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point (0,1). For this, we need to find dydx, which means we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=cos⁡tsin⁡t,y′(t)=−cos⁡tsin2⁡t.

So, we have dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=−cos⁡tsin2⁡t⋅sin⁡tcos⁡t=−1sin⁡t.

At the point where t=π2, the slope m of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=π/2=−1sin⁡(π2)=−1.

To find the slope mn of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of m:

mn=−1m=−1(−1)=1

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(0,1) and the slope mn=1. We get

y−1=1⋅(x−0)y=x+1.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The normal is horizontal if the tangent is vertical. Therefore, we require $x'(t)=0$ while $y'(t) \neq 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving $x'(t) = 0$ gives

$$
6t^2 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t = 0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =2\cdot 0-1=-1\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when $t = 0.$

Question 17
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t4+2t2,y=t3−3t,−∞<t<∞. Determine the value of the parameter t at which the normal line to the curve is horizontal.

a
t=0
b
t=2
c
t=−3
d
t=4
e
t=1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The normal line is horizontal when the tangent line to the curve is vertical. Therefore, we require x′(t)=0 while y′(t)≠0.

So, we first find the derivatives of x and y: x′(t)=4t3+4t,y′(t)=3t2−3

Solving x′(t)=0 gives 4t(t2+1)=0⟹t=0.

Now, we note that y′(0)=3(0)2−3=−3≠0, which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when t=0.

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-{e}^{-t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=10t
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
10t=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(0)=-{e}^{-0}=-1\ne 0,\,\,
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed vertical when $t=0.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{2}+8t,\,y=4{t}^{7},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=2t2+8t,y=4t7,−∞<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−2=7(x−10)
b
y−4=143(x−3)
c
y+2=76(x−10)
d
y−4=73(x−10)
e
y+4=37(x−10)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=2(1)2+8(1)=2+8=10,y=4(1)7=4.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (10,4).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=4t+8,y′(t)=28t6.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=28t64t+8.

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=28⋅(1)64⋅(1)+8=73.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(10,4) and the slope m=73. We get y−4=73(x−10).

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 1
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=2t2+8t,y=4t7,−∞<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−2=7(x−10)
b
y−4=143(x−3)
c
y+2=76(x−10)
d
y−4=73(x−10)
e
y+4=37(x−10)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=2(1)2+8(1)=2+8=10,y=4(1)7=4.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (10,4).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=4t+8,y′(t)=28t6.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=28t64t+8.

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=28⋅(1)64⋅(1)+8=73.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(10,4) and the slope m=73. We get y−4=73(x−10).
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve

solution.reasoning: At t=1, (x,y)=(10,4). The tangent slope is (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)=28t^6/(4t+8)=7/3 at t=1. Thus the tangent is y-4=\frac{7}{3}(x-10), option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{2}+8t,\,y=4{t}^{7},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2(1)^{2}+8(1)=2+8=10, \\ y & =4(1)^{7}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(10,4).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t+8,\,{y}^{′}(t)=28{t}^{6}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{28{t}^{6}}{4t+8}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =\frac{28\cdot (1)^{6}}{4\cdot (1)+8} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,4)$ and the slope $m=\frac{7}{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-4 & =\frac{7}{3}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=2t2+8t,y=4t7,−∞<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−2=7(x−10)
b
y−4=143(x−3)
c
y+2=76(x−10)
d
y−4=73(x−10)
e
y+4=37(x−10)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=2(1)2+8(1)=2+8=10,y=4(1)7=4.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (10,4).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=4t+8,y′(t)=28t6.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=28t64t+8.

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=28⋅(1)64⋅(1)+8=73.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(10,4) and the slope m=73. We get y−4=73(x−10).

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+3t,\,y=1+\sqrt{2t},\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=2$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=2$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(0,\,\frac{16}{7})$ is the $y$-intercept.

question.html:
Question 2
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t2+3t,y=1+2t,t∈[0,∞). Let C be the point that corresponds to t=2 on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at C crosses the y-axis.

a
(0,−57)
b
(0,167)
c
(0,−27)
d
(0,127)
e
(0,165)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=2 into the parametric equations: x=(2)2+3(2)=10,y=1+2(2)=3.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point (10,3).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=2t+3,y′(t)=12t.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=12t2t+3=12t(2t+3).

At the point where t=2, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=2=12⋅2(2⋅2+3)=114.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(10,3) and the slope m=114. We get y−3=114(x−10).

The tangent crosses the y-axis when x=0. At this point, we have

y−3=114(0−10)y−3=−57y=167.

Consequently, (0,167) is the y-intercept.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=2$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(0,\,\frac{16}{7})$ is the $y$-intercept.

question.problem:

Question 2
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t2+3t,y=1+2t,t∈[0,∞). Let C be the point that corresponds to t=2 on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at C crosses the y-axis.

a
(0,−57)
b
(0,167)
c
(0,−27)
d
(0,127)
e
(0,165)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=2 into the parametric equations: x=(2)2+3(2)=10,y=1+2(2)=3.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point (10,3).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=2t+3,y′(t)=12t.

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=12t2t+3=12t(2t+3).

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+3t,\,y=1+\sqrt{2t},\,t\in [0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=2$ on the curve. Determine the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=2$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(2)^{2}+3(2)=10, \\ y & =1+\sqrt{2(2)}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(10,3).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+3,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}}}{2t+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2t}(2t+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=2,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}(2\cdot 2+3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{14}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(10,3)$ and the slope $m=\frac{1}{14}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(x-10).\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =\frac{1}{14}(0-10) \\ y-3 & =-\frac{5}{7} \\ y & =\frac{16}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(0,\,\frac{16}{7})$ is the $y$-intercept.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{5}-4{t}^{3},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$

The Cartesian equation of the tangent line is $y=$
{{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(-2,1).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the Cartesian equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope $m=-1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =-(x+2) \\ y & =-x-2+1 \\ y & =-x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the tangent line  in slope-intercept form is $y=-x-1.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=\sqrt{t+1},\,y={t}^{3}+4,\,-1<t<\infty .
$$

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2}, \\ y & =(1)^{3}+4=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},5).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}})} \\  & =6{t}^{2}\sqrt{(t+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =6\cdot {1}^{2}\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\sqrt{2},5)$ and the slope $m=6\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5 & =6\sqrt{2}(x-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t+1,y=t3+4,−1<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−5=62(x−2)
b
y+2=324(x+5)
c
y+5=23(x+2)
d
y−5=2(x−2)
e
y−5=6(x−2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=1+1=2,y=(1)3+4=5.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (2,5).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=12t+1,y′(t)=3t2.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=3t2(12t+1)=6t2(t+1).

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=6⋅121+1=62.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(2,5) and the slope m=62. We get y−5=62(x−2).

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Tangent Line to a Parametric Curve
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt{2}, \\ y & =(1)^{3}+4=5.\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\sqrt{2},5).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}}{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t+1}})} \\  & =6{t}^{2}\sqrt{(t+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =6\cdot {1}^{2}\sqrt{1+1} \\  & =6\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(\sqrt{2},5)$ and the slope $m=6\sqrt{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5 & =6\sqrt{2}(x-\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t+1,y=t3+4,−1<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−5=62(x−2)
b
y+2=324(x+5)
c
y+5=23(x+2)
d
y−5=2(x−2)
e
y−5=6(x−2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=1+1=2,y=(1)3+4=5.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (2,5).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=12t+1,y′(t)=3t2.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=3t2(12t+1)=6t2(t+1).

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=6⋅121+1=62.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(2,5) and the slope m=62. We get y−5=62(x−2).

solution.reasoning: At t=1, the point is (\sqrt{2},5). Since dx/dt=1/(2\sqrt{t+1}) and dy/dt=3t^2, the tangent slope is 6t^2\sqrt{t+1}=6\sqrt{2}. Therefore y-5=6\sqrt{2}(x-\sqrt{2}), option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

Question 4

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=t+1,y=t3+4,−1<t<∞.

Calculate the equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where t=1.

a
y−5=62(x−2)
b
y+2=324(x+5)
c
y+5=23(x+2)
d
y−5=2(x−2)
e
y−5=6(x−2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting t=1 into the parametric equations: x=1+1=2,y=(1)3+4=5.

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent at the point (2,5).

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find dydx. To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=12t+1,y′(t)=3t2.

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=3t2(12t+1)=6t2(t+1).

At the point where t=1, the slope of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=1=6⋅121+1=62.

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(2,5) and the slope m=62. We get y−5=62(x−2).

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}t+\frac{3}{2},\,y={t}^{3}+7{t}^{2}+8t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=-1$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)+\frac{3}{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+7(-1)^{2}+8(-1)=-1+7-8=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,-2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}+14t+8}{2t+\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}+14(-1)+8}{2(-1)+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,-2)$ and the slope $m=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =2(x-2) \\ y+2 & =2x-4 \\ y & =2x-4-2 \\ y & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)-6 \\ y & =0-6 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-6).$

feedback.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}t+\frac{3}{2},\,y={t}^{3}+7{t}^{2}+8t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=-1$ on the curve. Determine the coordinates of the point at which the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis. Do not round the answers.

The tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}},
{{field-2}}$).$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=-1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =(-1)^{2}+\frac{1}{2}(-1)+\frac{3}{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2 \\ y & =(-1)^{3}+7(-1)^{2}+8(-1)=-1+7-8=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(2,-2).$ 

To find the equation of the tangent line, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}.$ To compute it, we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{3{t}^{2}+14t+8}{2t+\frac{1}{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=-1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,-1} & =\frac{3(-1)^{2}+14(-1)+8}{2(-1)+\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to calculate the equation of the tangent line, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,-2)$ and the slope $m=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =2(x-2) \\ y+2 & =2x-4 \\ y & =2x-4-2 \\ y & =2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent crosses the $y$-axis when $x=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2(0)-6 \\ y & =0-6 \\ y & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the tangent to the curve at $C$ crosses the $y$-axis at  $(0,\,-6).$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2(t+1),\,y=4{t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is horizontal.
question.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is horizontal if ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2,\,{y}^{′}(t)=8t.
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
8t=0\,⟹\,t=0.
$$

Note that ${x}^{′}(0)=2\ne 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that when $t=0,$ the tangent to the curve is horizontal.

Question 6
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=2(t+1),y=4t2,−∞<t<∞. Determine the value of t at which the tangent to the curve is horizontal.

a
 t=0
b
 t=−1
c
 t=−2
d
 t=3
e
 t=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The slope m of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

m=y′(t)x′(t).

The tangent line is horizontal if y′(t)=0 while x′(t)≠0.

So, we first find the derivatives of x and y:

x′(t)=2,y′(t)=8t.

Solving y′(t)=0 gives

8t=0⟹t=0.

Note that x′(0)=2≠0. Therefore, we conclude that when t=0, the tangent to the curve is horizontal.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={t}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}t+\frac{1}{2},\,y={t}^{3}+7{t}^{2}+8t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is horizontal. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the tangent to the curve is horizontal at $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is horizontal if ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2t+\frac{1}{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}+14t+8
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}+14t+8 & =0 \\ (3t+2)(t+4) & =0 \\ t & =-4,-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(-4) & =2(-4)+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{15}{2}\ne 0, \\ {x}^{′}(-\frac{2}{3}) & =2(-\frac{2}{3})+\frac{1}{2}=-\frac{5}{6}\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the tangent to the curve is indeed horizontal at $t=-4$ and $t=-\frac{2}{3}.$

question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=3{t}^{4},\,y=8t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Determine the value of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical.

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.

$$

$$

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=3t4,y=8t,−∞<t<∞. Determine the value of t at which the tangent to the curve is vertical.

a

t=−8
c

d
t=8

The slope m of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

Solving x′(t)=0 gives

Note that y′(0)=8≠0. Therefore, we conclude that when t=0 the tangent to the curve is vertical.

A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x={t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}+12t,\,y=4{t}^{2}-3t,\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

{{field-1}}.

$$

Now, we note that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(2) & =8(2)-3\ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=2.$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Determine the values of $t$ at which the tangent to the curve is vertical. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is vertical if ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)),\,{y}^{′}(t)={e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(t))
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =0 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =0 \\ 0 & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t) \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)} & =1 \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡(t)=1 \\ t & =\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{5\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we note that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})]=\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{\pi }{4}}\ne 0, \\ {y}^{′}(\frac{5\pi }{4}) & ={e}^{\frac{5\pi }{4}}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{4})]=-\sqrt{2}{e}^{\frac{5\pi }{4}}\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the tangent to the curve is vertical at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $t=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=2{t}^{5}-4{t}^{3},\,y={t}^{2},\,-\infty <t<\infty .
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=1$ on the curve. Find the Cartesian equation of the normal to the curve at $C.$

The Cartesian equation of the normal line at $C$ is $y=$
{{field-1}}.
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2({1}^{5})-4({1}^{3})=2-4=-2 \\ y & ={1}^{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we're looking to find the equation of the normal at the point $(-2,1).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t}{10{t}^{4}-12{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t\,=\,1} & =\frac{2(1)}{10({1}^{4})-12({1}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{2}{10-12} \\  & =\frac{2}{(-2)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m:$

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-1)\,}=1
$$

Finally, to find the Cartesian equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-2,1)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =1(x-(-2)) \\ y-1 & =x+2 \\ y & =x+2+1 \\ y & =x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the equation of the normal line  in slope-intercept form is $y=x+3.$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi }),\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\pi $ on the curve. Determine the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $x$-axis.
question.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\pi $ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-\pi )$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-\pi ) & =4(x-0) \\ y & =4x-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The normal intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\pi  & =0 \\ 4x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ is the $x$-intercept.

question.html:
Question 12
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=4tln⁡(tπ),y=tcos⁡t,t∈(0,∞).

Let C be the point that corresponds to t=π on the curve. Determine the point at which the normal to the curve at C crosses the x-axis.

a
(π4,0)
b
(π2,0)
c
(1,0)
d
(−1,0)
e
(−π,0)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=π into the parametric equations: x=4πln⁡(ππ)=4π(0)=0,y=πcos⁡π=−π

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point (0,−π). For this, we need to find dydx, which means we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=4ln⁡(tπ)+4,y′(t)=cos⁡(t)−tsin⁡t

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=cos⁡(t)−tsin⁡t4ln⁡(tπ)+4.

At the point where t=π, the slope m of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=π=cos⁡(π)−πsin⁡π4ln⁡(ππ)+4=−14⋅0+4=−14.

To find the slope mn of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of m:

mn=−1m=−1(−14)=4

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(0,−π) and the slope mn=4. We get

y−(−π)=4(x−0)y=4x−π. The normal intersects the x-axis when y=0. At this point, we have 4x−π=04x=πx=π4.

Consequently, (π4,0) is the x-intercept.

last_observation.name: Question 12
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\pi $ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-\pi )$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-\pi ) & =4(x-0) \\ y & =4x-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The normal intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\pi  & =0 \\ 4x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ is the $x$-intercept.

question.html:
Question 12
?

A curve is defined by the parametric equations x=4tln⁡(tπ),y=tcos⁡t,t∈(0,∞).

Let C be the point that corresponds to t=π on the curve. Determine the point at which the normal to the curve at C crosses the x-axis.

a
(π4,0)
b
(π2,0)
c
(1,0)
d
(−1,0)
e
(−π,0)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the coordinates of the point C by substituting t=π into the parametric equations: x=4πln⁡(ππ)=4π(0)=0,y=πcos⁡π=−π

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point (0,−π). For this, we need to find dydx, which means we first need to find the derivatives of x and y, as follows:

x′(t)=4ln⁡(tπ)+4,y′(t)=cos⁡(t)−tsin⁡t

So, we have

dydx=y′(t)x′(t)=cos⁡(t)−tsin⁡t4ln⁡(tπ)+4.

At the point where t=π, the slope m of the tangent line is given by m=dydx|t=π=cos⁡(π)−πsin⁡π4ln⁡(ππ)+4=−14⋅0+4=−14.

To find the slope mn of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of m:

mn=−1m=−1(−14)=4

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point (x1,y1)=(0,−π) and the slope mn=4. We get

y−(−π)=4(x−0)y=4x−π. The normal intersects the x-axis when y=0. At this point, we have 4x−π=04x=πx=π4.

Consequently, (π4,0) is the x-intercept.
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Normal Line to a Parametric Curve

solution.reasoning: At t=\pi, C=(0,-\pi). The derivatives are x'(t)=4\ln(t/\pi)+4 and y'(t)=\cos t-t\sin t, giving tangent slope -1/4 and normal slope 4. The normal is y+\pi=4x, so setting y=0 gives x=\pi/4, option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 12
feedback.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=4t\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi }),\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\in (0,\infty ).
$$

Let $C$ be the point that corresponds to $t=\pi $ on the curve. Determine the point at which the normal to the curve at $C$ crosses the $x$-axis.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=\pi $ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\pi \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })=4\pi (0)=0, \\ y & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to determine the equation of the normal at the point $(0,-\pi ).$ For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{t}{\pi })+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the slope $m$ of the tangent line is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=\pi } & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi }{4\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{\pi }{\pi })+4} \\  & =\frac{-1}{4\cdot 0+4}=-\,\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,(-\frac{1}{4})\,}=4
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(0,-\pi )$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-\pi ) & =4(x-0) \\ y & =4x-\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

The normal intersects the $x$-axis when $y=0.$ At this point, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-\pi  & =0 \\ 4x & =\pi  \\ x & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $(\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ is the $x$-intercept.
