observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing and Evaluating Triple Integrals Over Type III Regions From Diagrams
observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/71f3fd0cbbde8adeca71688d6b53e2cd4cdf72076be3efa770cfebb8c10ffb76.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/cd84968e9e5300a18d087ba566202aba2b7166818a590cca03eac90d4f3f7a89.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}8x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x[y]_{y=0}^{y=3-3x/4-z/2}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x(3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[24xz-6{x}^{2}z-2x{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(72x-18{x}^{2}-18x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[27{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(27-6)-0 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/9165163be9ce95e7165f04d26e6ce8080699ab4d477eba3f804c849fdf1fb679.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/ca74bf149c1371fe9f1622586d9eb92fe180a9c9bb6a0c53d16f538b3c55f4a4.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4{x}^{2}z\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z[y]_{y=0}^{y=4-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z(4-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[8{x}^{2}{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{x}^{2}{z}^{3}]_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx & ={[12{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(12-0) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Evaluate the triple integral ∭R4x2zdV over the region R, shown above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the right one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.

a
12
b
2
c
6
d
24
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,0≤y≤4−z},

where

D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤3}

is the projection of R onto the xz-plane, shown below.

Hence, the type III representation of R is

R={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤3,0≤y≤4−z}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭R4x2zdV=∫01∫03∫04−z4x2zdydzdx.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to y, treating x and z as constants:

∫01∫03∫04−z4x2zdydzdx=∫01∫03[∫04−z4x2zdy]dzdx=∫01∫034x2z[y]y=0y=4−zdzdx=∫01∫034x2z(4−z)dzdx=∫01∫03(16x2z−4x2z2)dzdx

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating x as a constant:

∫01∫03(16x2z−4x2z2)dzdx=∫01[∫03(16x2z−4x2z2)dz]dx=∫01[8x2z2−43x2z3]z=0z=3dx=∫0136x2dx

Finally, we integrate with respect to x:

∫0136x2dx=[12x3]x=0x=1=(12−0)=12.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/b176bcf502a0801eae2bf470dfe4bf92852a34b06675fd74be78b30ccb4f6469.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 3\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/eb054b5f1567aa2c56842d79133fbbefc41a8b40730c688381d88e3ef06ccab7.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}xz[y]_{y=1}^{y=3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}2xz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing and Evaluating Triple Integrals Over Type III Regions From Diagrams
observed_steps.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2f1112a1fa4e540ce8ef2d1337383a2adcb378ba519cfb9c49a4521e5bc1b02f.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the left curve

$$
x={z}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2dcbae12ed3351892c63117f86bab7ffe6e1818b7a16666b42c2efdcc6bd787f.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,{z}^{2}\le x\le 1\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}3\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20

Given that R is the type III region shown above, ∭R2ydV=

a
 ∫01∫z212xdxdz
b
 ∫01∫z21x2dxdz
c
 ∫01∫013dxdz
d
 ∫01∫01x2dxdz
e
∫01∫z213dxdz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a type III region R with projection D onto the xz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

We consider the region R as a type III region enclosed between the back surface y=u1(x,z)=1 and the front surface y=u2(x,z)=2.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,1≤y≤2}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type II plane region in the xz-plane with the left curve

x=z2.

Hence, D={(x,z):0≤z≤1,z2≤x≤1}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭R2ydV=∬D[∫122ydy]dA=∫01∫z21[∫122ydy]dxdz=∫01∫z21[y2]y=1y=2dxdz=∫01∫z213dxdz

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the type III region $R,$ given by

$$
S=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 2+{z}^{2}\},
$$

where $D$ is some finite region in the $xz$-plane. Then,

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V=
$$
question.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2},\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=2+{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the type III region R, given by S={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,x2≤y≤2+z2}, where D is some finite region in the xz-plane. Then, ∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∬D[∫x22+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫2+z2x2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫z22+x2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
d
∫x22+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
e
∫x22+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=x2,u2(x,z)=2+z2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫x22+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

last_observation.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2},\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=2+{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

$$

$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the type III region R, given by S={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,x2≤y≤2+z2}, where D is some finite region in the xz-plane. Then, ∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∬D[∫x22+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫2+z2x2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫z22+x2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
d
∫x22+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
e
∫x22+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=x2,u2(x,z)=2+z2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫x22+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

solution.reasoning: For each fixed (x,z) in D, integrate first with respect to y from x² to 2+z², then integrate over D in the xz-plane. This gives option a. The supplied example supports this rule, but no Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2},\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=2+{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

a
∬D[∫x22+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫2+z2x2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫z22+x2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
d
∫x22+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
e
∫x22+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dz]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=x2,u2(x,z)=2+z2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫x22+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

question.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=-z,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)={x}^{2}+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-z}^{{x}^{2}+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Consider the type III region R, given by S={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,−z≤y≤x2+z}, where D is some finite region in the xz-plane. Then, ∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫−zx2+z[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫−zx2+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫x2+z−zf(x,y,z)dy]dz
d
∬D[∫−zx2+zf(x,y,z)dz]dA
e
∬D[∫x2+z−zf(x,y,z)dy]dA
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=−z,u2(x,z)=x2+z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−zx2+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=-z,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)={x}^{2}+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-z}^{{x}^{2}+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the type III region R, given by S={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,−z≤y≤x2+z}, where D is some finite region in the xz-plane. Then, ∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫−zx2+z[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫−zx2+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫x2+z−zf(x,y,z)dy]dz
d
∬D[∫−zx2+zf(x,y,z)dz]dA
e
∬D[∫x2+z−zf(x,y,z)dy]dA
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=−z,u2(x,z)=x2+z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−zx2+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA.

solution.reasoning: Integrate first with respect to y from its lower boundary −z to its upper boundary x²+z, then integrate over D in the xz-plane. Thus option b is mathematically correct. No answer or grade for this current question is captured to establish Math Academy's key.

feedback.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=-z,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)={x}^{2}+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-z}^{{x}^{2}+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=−z,u2(x,z)=x2+z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−zx2+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA.

question.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2}-2,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}-2}^{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the type III region R, given by S={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,x2−2≤y≤x2+z2}, where D is some finite region in the xz-plane. Then, ∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫x2−2x2+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫x2z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫x2+2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dz]dA
d
∫x2+2x2+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
e
∬D[∫x2−2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=x2−2,u2(x,z)=x2+z2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫x2−2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2}-2,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}-2}^{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the type III region R, given by S={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,x2−2≤y≤x2+z2}, where D is some finite region in the xz-plane. Then, ∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫x2−2x2+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫x2z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫x2+2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dz]dA
d
∫x2+2x2+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
e
∬D[∫x2−2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=x2−2,u2(x,z)=x2+z2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫x2−2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

solution.reasoning: For each fixed (x,z) in D, integrate with respect to y from x²−2 to x²+z², then integrate over D in the xz-plane. This is option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)={x}^{2}-2,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}-2}^{{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

Consider the type III region R, given by S={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,x2−2≤y≤x2+z2}, where D is some finite region in the xz-plane. Then, ∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫x2−2x2+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
b
∬D[∫x2z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
c
∬D[∫x2+2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dz]dA
d
∫x2+2x2+z2[∬Df(x,y,z)dy]dA
e
∬D[∫x2−2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=x2−2,u2(x,z)=x2+z2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫x2−2x2+z2f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{∗}^{∗}{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx
$$

The triple integral above is defined over the type III region given by

$$
S=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le z\le 2x+1,\,0\le y\le 1+x+z\}.
$$

What is the value of $a+b?$
question.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=0,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=1+x+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

 

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le z\le 2x+1\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2x+1}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dz\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2x+1}{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=(-1)+(2x+1)=2x.
$$

a
x+z
b
2x
c
1
d
0
e
2x+1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=0,u2(x,z)=1+x+z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA.

Now, the region D is given by

D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,−1≤z≤2x+1}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get

∬D[∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA=∫01∫12x+1[∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dzdx=∫01∫−12x+1∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dydzdx.

Finally,

a+b=(−1)+(2x+1)=2x.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=0,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=1+x+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

 

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le z\le 2x+1\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2x+1}[{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dz\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2x+1}{\int }_{0}^{1+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=(-1)+(2x+1)=2x.
$$

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∫∗∗∫ab∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dydzdx The triple integral above is defined over the type III region given by S={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,−1≤z≤2x+1,0≤y≤1+x+z}. What is the value of a+b?

a
x+z
b
2x
c
1
d
0
e
2x+1
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=0,u2(x,z)=1+x+z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA.

Now, the region D is given by

D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,−1≤z≤2x+1}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get

∬D[∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA=∫01∫12x+1[∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dzdx=∫01∫−12x+1∫01+x+zf(x,y,z)dydzdx.

Finally,

a+b=(−1)+(2x+1)=2x.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{∗}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}{\int }_{∗}^{b}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx
$$

The triple integral above is defined over the type III region given by

$$
S=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-2\le z\le {x}^{2}+2,\,-2-z\le y\le 2+x+z\}.
$$

What is the value of $a-b?$
question.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=-2-z,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=2+x+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

 

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-2\le z\le {x}^{2}+2\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{{x}^{2}+2}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dz\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{{x}^{2}+2}{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a-b=(0)-(2+x+z)=-2-x-z.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∫a∗∫∗∗∫∗bf(x,y,z)dydzdx The triple integral above is defined over the type III region given by S={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,−2≤z≤x2+2,−2−z≤y≤2+x+z}. What is the value of a−b?

a
2−z−x
b
z+x
c
−2−z
d
−2−x−z
e
−2−x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=−2−z,u2(x,z)=2+x+z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA.

Now, the region D is given by

D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,−2≤z≤x2+2}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get

∬D[∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA=∫01∫−2x2+2[∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dzdx=∫01∫−2x2+2∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dydzdx.

Finally,

a−b=(0)−(2+x+z)=−2−x−z.
question.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral

last_observation.worked_solution:
A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(x,z)\le y\le {u}_{2}(x,z)\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/0603bed12c6af74e46544d8bebc52362aed95a9a5ad7418ea4faaf228f3b5241.png)

 

If $R$ is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(x,z)=-2-z,\,{u}_{2}(x,z)=2+x+z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA.
$$

 

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,-2\le z\le {x}^{2}+2\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{{x}^{2}+2}[{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy]dz\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-2}^{{x}^{2}+2}{\int }_{-2-z}^{2+x+z}f(x,y,z)\,dy\,dz\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a-b=(0)-(2+x+z)=-2-x-z.
$$

Question 5
?

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∫a∗∫∗∗∫∗bf(x,y,z)dydzdx The triple integral above is defined over the type III region given by S={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,−2≤z≤x2+2,−2−z≤y≤2+x+z}. What is the value of a−b?

a
2−z−x
b
z+x
c
−2−z
d
−2−x−z
e
−2−x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type III region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,u1(x,z)≤y≤u2(x,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type III region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type III region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA

In our case, we have

u1(x,z)=−2−z,u2(x,z)=2+x+z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

∭Sf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA.

Now, the region D is given by

D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,−2≤z≤x2+2}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get

∬D[∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dA=∫01∫−2x2+2[∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dy]dzdx=∫01∫−2x2+2∫−2−z2+x+zf(x,y,z)dydzdx.

Finally,

a−b=(0)−(2+x+z)=−2−x−z.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le z\le 2-x\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}2x[y]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region in the $xz$-plane.
Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $z$ and then with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-x}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2-x}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}{[z]}_{z=0}^{z=2-x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}(2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(\frac{32}{3}-8)-0 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Evaluate the mixed integral ∬D[∫0x2xdy]dA given that the region D in the xz-plane is given by D={(x,z):0≤x≤2,0≤z≤2−x}.

a
83
b
3
c
12
d
34
e
23
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to y, treating x and z as constants:

∬D[∫0x2xdy]dA=∬D2x[y]y=0y=xdA=∬D2x2dA

Notice that D is a type I region in the xz-plane. Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to z and then with respect to x:

∬D2x2dA=∫02∫02−x2x2dzdx=∫022x2[∫02−xdz]dx=∫022x2[z]z=0z=2−xdx=∫022x2(2−x)dx=∫02(4x2−2x3)dx=[43x3−12x4]x=0x=2=(323−8)−0=83
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Mixed Integral

solution.reasoning: The inner integral is 2x². Integrating over D gives ∫₀²2x²(2−x) dx = [4x³/3−x⁴/2]₀² = 8/3, option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for the current question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le z\le 2-x\}.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2x\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}2x[y]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region in the $xz$-plane.
Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $z$ and then with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-x}2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2-x}\,\text{d}z]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}{[z]}_{z=0}^{z=2-x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{x}^{2}(2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(\frac{32}{3}-8)-0 \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}4zy\,dy]dA,
$$

Evaluate the repeated integral above given that $D$ is a region in the $xz$-plane bounded by the lines $z=0,$ $x=2$ and the line $z-x=0.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}4zy\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}2z[{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2zx\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to calculate this double integral, we plot $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/b748f589d7fa773444fc45bdbd1d94a5424bb81c40851f0f0f2542a4f66c0c8d.png)

 

Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $z$ and then with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2zx\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}2zx\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =4-0 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}4zy\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}2z[{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2zx\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to calculate this double integral, we plot $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/b748f589d7fa773444fc45bdbd1d94a5424bb81c40851f0f0f2542a4f66c0c8d.png)

 

Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $z$ and then with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2zx\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}2zx\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =4-0 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/b748f589d7fa773444fc45bdbd1d94a5424bb81c40851f0f0f2542a4f66c0c8d.png)

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA,
$$

Evaluate the repeated integral above given that $D$ is a region in the $xz$-plane bounded by the lines $z=0,$ $x=0,$ and the curve $z+{x}^{2}=1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}2x[{y}^{2}]_{y=x}^{y=\sqrt{1-z}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(1-z-{x}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to calculate this double integral, we plot $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/8079d8f9796c1f863a515ced0091c1f420318be1c4bfe0eb2da641bddfa426ce.png)

 

Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $z$ and then with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x[-(1-z)^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}-2{x}^{3}[z]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}\,)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-{x}^{5}+x-2{x}^{3}+2{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{5}+x-2{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$

Now, to calculate this double integral, we plot $D$ as a type I plane region in the $xz$-plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/8079d8f9796c1f863a515ced0091c1f420318be1c4bfe0eb2da641bddfa426ce.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}(\,2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x[-(1-z)^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}-2{x}^{3}[z]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}\,)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-{x}^{5}+x-2{x}^{3}+2{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{5}+x-2{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}{x}^{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2xyz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-2z},\,0\le z\le 2\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{x}2xyz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}xz[{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{3}z\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type II region in the $xz$-plane.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}5yz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A
$$

given that the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane is given by

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 2,\,0\le x\le 2-z\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $z$ and $x$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}5yz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}5z{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{∬}_{D}z(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $D$ is a type II region in the $xz$-plane.
Therefore, to evaluate our double integral as a repeated integral over this region, we integrate with respect to $x$ and then with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}{∬}_{D}z(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-z}z(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z[{\int }_{0}^{2-z}(4-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z{[(4x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})]}_{x=0}^{x=2-z}\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z(4(2-z)-\frac{(2-z)^{3}}{3})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{16z}{3}-2{z}^{3}+\frac{{z}^{4}}{3})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[\frac{8{z}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{z}^{4}}{2}+\frac{{z}^{5}}{15}]}_{z=0}^{z=2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}[\frac{32}{3}-8+\frac{32}{15}] \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}3x\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le x,\,0\le z\le 2-x\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}3x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-x}{\int }_{0}^{x}3x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}xyz\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 2,\,0\le x\le \sqrt{4-2z},\,0\le y\le x\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}xyz\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy\,dx\,dz.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy\,dx\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xyz\,dy]dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}xz{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}xz(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})\,dx\,dz \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{x}^{3}z\,dx\,dz\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $z$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2x}}{x}^{3}z\,dx\,dz & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2z}}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}z{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{4-2z}}\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}(4-2z)^{2}z\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4z-4{z}^{2}+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $z:$

$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4z-4{z}^{2}+{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z & =\frac{1}{2}{[2{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{z}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(8-\frac{32}{3}+4)-0 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}4xy\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,x\le y\le \sqrt{1-z}\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $xz$-plane enclosed between the $x$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the curve $z=1-{x}^{2},$ in the first quadrant.
question.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4xy\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}2x[{y}^{2}]_{y=x}^{y=\sqrt{1-z}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(\,(1-z)-{x}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/95a2b4e28dbfae5ce447b3b975b2f74bf04883441217f42a24636970948402a0.png)

  

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-z}}2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,dx\,dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-z}}2x\,dx]dz+{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-z}}-2{x}^{3}\,dx]dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-z}}dz+{\int }_{0}^{1}{[-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-z}}dz \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)^{2}\,dz-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)^{2}\,dz \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(1-z)^{2}\,dz \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{[-(1-z)^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

where the region R is given by R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,x≤y≤1−z}, and D is a finite region in xz-plane enclosed between the x-axis, the z-axis, and the curve z=1−x2, in the first quadrant.

Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

∭R4xydV=∬D[∫x1−z4xydy]dA.

∬D[∫x1−z4xydy]dA=∬D2x[y2]y=xy=1−zdA=∬D2x((1−z)−x2)dA=∬D2x(1−z)−2x3dA

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

∬D2x(1−z)−2x3dA=∫01∫01−z2x(1−z)−2x3dxdz=∫01(1−z)[∫01−z2xdx]dz+∫01[∫01−z−2x3dx]dz=∫01(1−z)[x2]x=0x=1−zdz+∫01[−x42]x=0x=1−zdz=∫01(1−z)2dz−12∫01(1−z)2dz=12∫01(1−z)2dz=16[−(1−z)3]z=0z=1=16

where the region $R$ is given by

$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $xz$-plane enclosed between the $x$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the curve $z=1-{x}^{2},$ in the first quadrant.

$$
{∭}_{R}4xy\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{x}^{\sqrt{1-z}}4xy\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}2x[{y}^{2}]_{y=x}^{y=\sqrt{1-z}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(\,(1-z)-{x}^{2})\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x(1-z)-2{x}^{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/95a2b4e28dbfae5ce447b3b975b2f74bf04883441217f42a24636970948402a0.png)

$$

$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}20y\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type III region given by 

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{x}^{2},\,0\le y\le 1-x\}.
$$
question.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}20y\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}20y\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{0}^{1-x}20y\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}[10{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1-x}dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}10(1-x)^{2}\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}10(1-x)^{2}\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}10(1-x)^{2}\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10(1-x)^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10(1-x)^{2}(1-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10(1-2x+2{x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}10(1-2x+2{x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\,dx & ={[10(x-{x}^{2}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5})]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭R2xdV=∫01∫01−x2∫01−x20ydydzdx.

∫01∫01−x2∫01−x20ydydzdx=∫01∫01−x2[∫01−x20ydy]dzdx=∫01∫01−x2[10y2]y=0y=1−xdzdx=∫01∫01−x210(1−x)2dzdx

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}10(1-x)^{2}\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}10(1-x)^{2}\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10(1-x)^{2}[z]_{z=0}^{z=1-{x}^{2}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10(1-x)^{2}(1-{x}^{2})dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}10(1-2x+2{x}^{3}-{x}^{4})\,dx\end{aligned}

$$

Question 14
?

Evaluate the triple integral

∭R20ydV

where R is the type III region given by

R={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤1−x2,0≤y≤1−x}.

a
2
b
8
c
7

4
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭R2xdV=∫01∫01−x2∫01−x20ydydzdx.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to y, treating x and z as constants:

∫01∫01−x2∫01−x20ydydzdx=∫01∫01−x2[∫01−x20ydy]dzdx=∫01∫01−x2[10y2]y=0y=1−xdzdx=∫01∫01−x210(1−x)2dzdx

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating x as a constant:

∫01∫01−x210(1−x)2dzdx=∫01[∫01−x210(1−x)2dz]dx=∫0110(1−x)2[z]z=0z=1−x2dx=∫0110(1−x)2(1−x2)dx=∫0110(1−2x+2x3−x4)dx

Finally, we integrate with respect to x:

∫0110(1−2x+2x3−x4)dx=[10(x−x2+x42−x55)]x=0x=1=3.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}12y\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $xz$-plane enclosed between the $x$-axis, the line $x=1,$ and the line $z=x$ in the first quadrant.
question.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}12y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}12y\,dy]dA.
$$

 

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}12y\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}6[{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}6x\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

 

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/1d102b63c3deb8121ea88cdc994b9410cf28f9c3bb29abc5ea4a14d7e1e7c389.png)

 

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}6x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}6x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6x[z]_{z=0}^{z=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}12y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}12y\,dy]dA.
$$

 

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}12y\,dy]dA & ={∬}_{D}6[{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}6x\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

 

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $xz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/1d102b63c3deb8121ea88cdc994b9410cf28f9c3bb29abc5ea4a14d7e1e7c389.png)

 

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}6x\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}6x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6x[z]_{z=0}^{z=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the triple integral

∭R12ydV

where the region R is given by R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,0≤y≤x}, and D is a finite region in xz-plane enclosed between the x-axis, the line x=1, and the line z=x in the first quadrant.

a
12
b
32
c
52
d
1
e
2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

∭R12ydV=∬D[∫0x12ydy]dA.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to y, treating x and z as constants:

∬D[∫0x12ydy]dA=∬D6[y2]y=0y=xdA=∬D6xdA

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region D in the xz-plane shown below.

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

∬D6xdA=∫01∫0x6xdzdx=∫016x[z]z=0z=xdx=∫016x2dx=[2x3]x=0x=1=2

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/3cba44923f4f583cf6e01ac87cdd6e5ca73a75993eef8322cd01bf44416f84f4.png)

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}4x\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the right one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/f112dd83a8cbb7563979dc170db23db7e178ba1762aca23fd4073c50e1c7a343.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 5-x-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/71974fddc8e0e0b6a12fc6a248c15eea08c9f6b8a0823d50aede8aadc31a41fa.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 5-x-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4x[y]_{y=0}^{y=5-x-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4x(5-x-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[20xz-4{x}^{2}z-2x{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(32x-8{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(32x-8{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[16{x}^{2}-\frac{8{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(64-\frac{64}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{128}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 16
?

Evaluate the triple integral ∭R4xdV over the region R, shown above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the right one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.

a
4
b
−13
c
1283
d
−1
e
−52
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,0≤y≤5−x−z},

where

D={(x,z):0≤x≤2,0≤z≤2}

is the projection of R onto the xz-plane, shown below.

Hence, the type III representation of R is

R={(x,y,z):0≤x≤2,0≤z≤2,0≤y≤5−x−z}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭R4xdV=∫02∫02∫05−x−z4xdydzdx.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to y, treating x and z as constants:

∫02∫02∫05−x−z4xdydzdx=∫02∫02[∫05−x−z4xdy]dzdx=∫02∫024x[y]y=0y=5−x−zdzdx=∫02∫024x(5−x−z)dzdx=∫02∫02(20x−4x2−4xz)dzdx

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating x as a constant:

∫02∫02(20x−4x2−4xz)dzdx=∫02[∫02(20x−4x2−4xz)dz]dx=∫02[20xz−4x2z−2xz2]z=0z=2dx=∫03(32x−8x2)dx

Finally, we integrate with respect to x:

∫02(32x−8x2)dx=[16x2−8x33]x=0x=2=(64−643)−0=1283.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/f112dd83a8cbb7563979dc170db23db7e178ba1762aca23fd4073c50e1c7a343.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 5-x-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/71974fddc8e0e0b6a12fc6a248c15eea08c9f6b8a0823d50aede8aadc31a41fa.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 5-x-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{5-x-z}4x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4x[y]_{y=0}^{y=5-x-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}4x(5-x-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2}(20x-4{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[20xz-4{x}^{2}z-2x{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(32x-8{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(32x-8{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[16{x}^{2}-\frac{8{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =(64-\frac{64}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{128}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/cd84968e9e5300a18d087ba566202aba2b7166818a590cca03eac90d4f3f7a89.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2}\}
$$

$$
{∭}_{R}8x\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3-3x/4-z/2}8x\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x[y]_{y=0}^{y=3-3x/4-z/2}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}8x(3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{z}{2})\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(24x-6{x}^{2}-4xz)\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[24xz-6{x}^{2}z-2x{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(72x-18{x}^{2}-18x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[27{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(27-6)-0 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

 

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(54x-18{x}^{2})\,dx & ={[27{x}^{2}-6{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(27-6)-0 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/9165163be9ce95e7165f04d26e6ce8080699ab4d477eba3f804c849fdf1fb679.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/ca74bf149c1371fe9f1622586d9eb92fe180a9c9bb6a0c53d16f538b3c55f4a4.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4{x}^{2}z\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z[y]_{y=0}^{y=4-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z(4-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[8{x}^{2}{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{x}^{2}{z}^{3}]_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx & ={[12{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(12-0) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/9165163be9ce95e7165f04d26e6ce8080699ab4d477eba3f804c849fdf1fb679.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\},
$$

where

$$
D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/ca74bf149c1371fe9f1622586d9eb92fe180a9c9bb6a0c53d16f538b3c55f4a4.png)

Hence, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 4-z\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4{x}^{2}z\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{4-z}4{x}^{2}z\,dy]dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z[y]_{y=0}^{y=4-z}\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}z(4-z)\,dz\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}(16{x}^{2}z-4{x}^{2}{z}^{2})\,dz]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[8{x}^{2}{z}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{x}^{2}{z}^{3}]_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}36{x}^{2}\,dx & ={[12{x}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=1} \\  & =(12-0) \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Evaluate the triple integral ∭R4x2zdV over the region R, shown above.

Hint: All surfaces, except for the right one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.

a
12
b
2
c
6
d
24
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that our solid can be written as the type III region

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,0≤y≤4−z},

where

D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤3}

is the projection of R onto the xz-plane, shown below.

Hence, the type III representation of R is

R={(x,y,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤3,0≤y≤4−z}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭R4x2zdV=∫01∫03∫04−z4x2zdydzdx.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to y, treating x and z as constants:

∫01∫03∫04−z4x2zdydzdx=∫01∫03[∫04−z4x2zdy]dzdx=∫01∫034x2z[y]y=0y=4−zdzdx=∫01∫034x2z(4−z)dzdx=∫01∫03(16x2z−4x2z2)dzdx

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating x as a constant:

∫01∫03(16x2z−4x2z2)dzdx=∫01[∫03(16x2z−4x2z2)dz]dx=∫01[8x2z2−43x2z3]z=0z=3dx=∫0136x2dx

Finally, we integrate with respect to x:

∫0136x2dx=[12x3]x=0x=1=(12−0)=12.

question.name: Question 19
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/335bf5e4e2a4ee9d0286eadb968e0e82c6afb18d47cd5258d6d1b6cee3d5c5a6.png)

Given that $R$ is the type III region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V=$
question.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/b176bcf502a0801eae2bf470dfe4bf92852a34b06675fd74be78b30ccb4f6469.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 3\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/eb054b5f1567aa2c56842d79133fbbefc41a8b40730c688381d88e3ef06ccab7.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}xz[y]_{y=1}^{y=3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}2xz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Given that R is the type III region shown above, ∭RxzdV=

a
∫01−x2∫01xz2dzdx
b
∫01∫032xzdzdx
c
∫01∫012xzdzdx
d
∫01∫01−x22xzdzdx
e
∫01∫01−x2xz2dzdx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a type III region R with projection D onto the xz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

We consider the region R as a type III region enclosed between the back surface y=u1(x,z)=1 and the front surface y=u2(x,z)=3.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,1≤y≤3}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type I plane region in the xz-plane with the upper curve

z=1−x2.

Hence, D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤1−x2}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭RxzdV=∬D[∫13xzdy]dA=∫01∫01−x2[∫13xzdy]dzdx=∫01∫01−x2xz[y]y=1y=3dzdx=∫01∫01−x22xzdzdx

last_observation.name: Question 19
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing and Evaluating Triple Integrals Over Type III Regions From Diagrams
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/b176bcf502a0801eae2bf470dfe4bf92852a34b06675fd74be78b30ccb4f6469.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 3\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/eb054b5f1567aa2c56842d79133fbbefc41a8b40730c688381d88e3ef06ccab7.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}xz[y]_{y=1}^{y=3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}2xz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Given that R is the type III region shown above, ∭RxzdV=

a
∫01−x2∫01xz2dzdx
b
∫01∫032xzdzdx
c
∫01∫012xzdzdx
d
∫01∫01−x22xzdzdx
e
∫01∫01−x2xz2dzdx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a type III region R with projection D onto the xz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

We consider the region R as a type III region enclosed between the back surface y=u1(x,z)=1 and the front surface y=u2(x,z)=3.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,1≤y≤3}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type I plane region in the xz-plane with the upper curve

z=1−x2.

Hence, D={(x,z):0≤x≤1,0≤z≤1−x2}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭RxzdV=∬D[∫13xzdy]dA=∫01∫01−x2[∫13xzdy]dzdx=∫01∫01−x2xz[y]y=1y=3dzdx=∫01∫01−x22xzdzdx
question.knowledge_point: Constructing and Evaluating Triple Integrals Over Type III Regions From Diagrams

solution.reasoning: The diagram shows 1≤y≤3, 0≤x≤1, and 0≤z≤1−x². Integrating xz with respect to y multiplies it by 3−1=2, giving option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/335bf5e4e2a4ee9d0286eadb968e0e82c6afb18d47cd5258d6d1b6cee3d5c5a6.png)

Given that $R$ is the type III region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V=$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/b176bcf502a0801eae2bf470dfe4bf92852a34b06675fd74be78b30ccb4f6469.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 3\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
z=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/eb054b5f1567aa2c56842d79133fbbefc41a8b40730c688381d88e3ef06ccab7.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le z\le 1-{x}^{2}\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}xz\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{1}^{3}xz\,\text{d}y]\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}xz[y]_{y=1}^{y=3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-{x}^{2}}2xz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/5b7552bbde56a68bfca44adb0501a4a4a8ae0a1105d3dc9039d05bfb6fd405c9.png)

Given that $R$ is the type III region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V=$
question.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2f1112a1fa4e540ce8ef2d1337383a2adcb378ba519cfb9c49a4521e5bc1b02f.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the left curve

$$
x={z}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2dcbae12ed3351892c63117f86bab7ffe6e1818b7a16666b42c2efdcc6bd787f.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,{z}^{2}\le x\le 1\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}3\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20
?

Given that R is the type III region shown above, ∭R2ydV=

a
 ∫01∫z212xdxdz
b
 ∫01∫z21x2dxdz
c
 ∫01∫013dxdz
d
 ∫01∫01x2dxdz
e
∫01∫z213dxdz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a type III region R with projection D onto the xz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

We consider the region R as a type III region enclosed between the back surface y=u1(x,z)=1 and the front surface y=u2(x,z)=2.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,1≤y≤2}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type II plane region in the xz-plane with the left curve

x=z2.

Hence, D={(x,z):0≤z≤1,z2≤x≤1}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭R2ydV=∬D[∫122ydy]dA=∫01∫z21[∫122ydy]dxdz=∫01∫z21[y2]y=1y=2dxdz=∫01∫z213dxdz

last_observation.name: Question 20
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing and Evaluating Triple Integrals Over Type III Regions From Diagrams
last_observation.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2f1112a1fa4e540ce8ef2d1337383a2adcb378ba519cfb9c49a4521e5bc1b02f.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the left curve

$$
x={z}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2dcbae12ed3351892c63117f86bab7ffe6e1818b7a16666b42c2efdcc6bd787f.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,{z}^{2}\le x\le 1\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}3\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20
?

Given that R is the type III region shown above, ∭R2ydV=

a
 ∫01∫z212xdxdz
b
 ∫01∫z21x2dxdz
c
 ∫01∫013dxdz
d
 ∫01∫01x2dxdz
e
∫01∫z213dxdz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a type III region R with projection D onto the xz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

We consider the region R as a type III region enclosed between the back surface y=u1(x,z)=1 and the front surface y=u2(x,z)=2.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,1≤y≤2}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type II plane region in the xz-plane with the left curve

x=z2.

Hence, D={(x,z):0≤z≤1,z2≤x≤1}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭R2ydV=∬D[∫122ydy]dA=∫01∫z21[∫122ydy]dxdz=∫01∫z21[y2]y=1y=2dxdz=∫01∫z213dxdz
question.knowledge_point: Constructing and Evaluating Triple Integrals Over Type III Regions From Diagrams

solution.reasoning: The visible shape suggests 0≤z≤1, z²≤x≤1, and constant y-limits, apparently 1≤y≤2. Under that interpretation, integrating 2y over y gives 2²−1²=3, producing option e. ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/5b7552bbde56a68bfca44adb0501a4a4a8ae0a1105d3dc9039d05bfb6fd405c9.png)

Given that $R$ is the type III region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V=$
feedback.worked_solution:
For a type III region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type III region enclosed between the back surface $y={u}_{1}(x,z)=1$ and the front surface $y={u}_{2}(x,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2f1112a1fa4e540ce8ef2d1337383a2adcb378ba519cfb9c49a4521e5bc1b02f.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R=\{(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,1\le y\le 2\}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type II *plane* region in the $xz$-plane with the left curve

$$
x={z}^{2}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14217845/assets/2dcbae12ed3351892c63117f86bab7ffe6e1818b7a16666b42c2efdcc6bd787f.png)

Hence, $D=\{(x,z)\,:\,0\le z\le 1,\,{z}^{2}\le x\le 1\}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2y\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}[{y}^{2}]_{y=1}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{z}^{2}}^{1}3\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

Question 20
?

Given that R is the type III region shown above, ∭R2ydV=

a
 ∫01∫z212xdxdz
b
 ∫01∫z21x2dxdz
c
 ∫01∫013dxdz
d
 ∫01∫01x2dxdz
e
∫01∫z213dxdz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a type III region R with projection D onto the xz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(x,z)u2(x,z)f(x,y,z)dy]dA.

We consider the region R as a type III region enclosed between the back surface y=u1(x,z)=1 and the front surface y=u2(x,z)=2.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(x,z)∈D,1≤y≤2}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type II plane region in the xz-plane with the left curve

x=z2.

Hence, D={(x,z):0≤z≤1,z2≤x≤1}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭R2ydV=∬D[∫122ydy]dA=∫01∫z21[∫122ydy]dxdz=∫01∫z21[y2]y=1y=2dxdz=∫01∫z213dxdz
